The international system is in disarray. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and the war in Gaza that began in October 2023 mark further steps in the erosion of the post-Cold War liberal international order. In hindsight, the promise of a global liberal era of peace and prosperity experienced its first setbacks already in the early 1990s. Failed United Nations (UN) operations in Somalia in 1993, Rwanda in 1994, and Bosnia in 1995 undermined international confidence in Western-style humanitarian universalism (see Barnett Citation 1997). Following the terrorist attacks of 9/11 in 2001, the United States and its “coalition of the willing” escalated its liberal-values-cum-security imperative to a more militarily proactive and less multilateral strategy. The resulting wars in Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003 showed that Western interventionism had reached and would soon surpass the peak of its post-Cold War expansion. In 2007, a global financial crisis plunged not just markets but also the political integration of the European Union (EU) into a deep crisis, reinforcing national antagonisms and undermining popular support for a deregulated globalized economy. In the same year, Russian President Vladimir Putin (Citation 2007) delivered a speech at the Munich Security Conference, where he openly attacked the Western-dominated international system. And while the UN developed a new concept, the “responsibility to protect”, when confronted with severe international crises such as the Syrian civil war beginning in 2011 or the Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014, it again faced the same constraints on its action in the shape of the Security Council vetoes and lack of both legitimacy and resolve that had plagued the organization during the Cold War.

Instead of Francis Fukuyama’s (Citation 1989) end time of universal liberal democracy, we have witnessed since about 2011 a proliferation of humanitarian crises, intensifying repression of political dissent and minorities by aggressive authoritarian regimes, and, recently, large-scale inter-state conflict (see Betts Citation 2019; cf. the much more optimistic assessment ten years earlier by Ash Citation 2009). At the same time, multilateral conflict management and global governance – once hailed to deliver humanity to an age of progress and peace – have been reduced to moral appeals and sporadic and often ineffective and illegitimate attempts to prevent the worst (see Coyne Citation 2013; Cunliffe Citation 2013; Darby Citation 2009; Hönke and Müller Citation 2012; Menon Citation 2016; Razack Citation 2004; Sabaratnam Citation 2017). This is a critical moment, therefore, to take stock of histories of foreign intervention and conflict management over the past century and consider their significance for international politics today.

The aim of this special issue is twofold. First, we seek to examine League of Nations and United Nations interventions in international conflicts and crises by identifying the causes, dynamics, and wider consequences of these interventions within a common analytical framework. Engaging with social science studies, we develop a more comprehensive and historically sensitive definition of foreign interventions and their successes and failures within changing “regimes” of global governance. Tracing the challenges interveners faced and the means they found to overcome, or rather circumvent, them, we demonstrate that the present crisis of the liberal international order has its roots in the crucial formative years of global governance between the 1920s and the 1970s. Our second aim is to use the study of these cases to identify larger historical trends and historical lessons, or, more modestly, reflection points, for policymakers and humanitarian workers today. What we have in mind is not limited to providing historical or cultural context for practitioners in their struggle to make sense of a region and conflict. What we seek to highlight, instead, are wider dynamics and patterns of conflicts at local, regional, national, and international levels and the risks and opportunities involved in external action and inaction.

Our five individual essays examine the challenges interveners faced, the strategies they adopted, and the consequences of their actions within different historical contexts. They investigate a variety of forms of foreign interventions carried out under the auspices of the League of Nations and the United Nations, spanning a large part of the globe and a large part of the twentieth century – from the formative stages of the international system that emerged after World War I to the later stages of decolonization in the 1970s. In the first essay, Barbara Warnock explores the attempts of the League of Nations to stabilize the Austrian economy after World War I, an early example of neoliberal fiscal intervention with highly ambivalent outcomes. Shifting our focus to global education and East Asia, Yarong Chen explores the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO’s) ambitious but ultimately futile involvement in China during the communist revolution. Turning to UN peacekeeping and the Middle East, Martin Jorgensen shows how the UN produced both insecurity and counterproductive “peacekeeping economies” in the Gaza Strip in the 1950s. In the fourth essay, Volker Prott explores the UN’s efforts to resolve the Kashmir dispute in the late 1940s, stabilize and modernize Congo in the early 1960s, and get involved in the East Pakistan crisis of 1971. Taking us to South-East Asia and the global politics of refugees, Sara Cosemans and Trinh Van Vinh unpack the troubled expansion of the work of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Vietnam between 1973 and 1979.

The concepts and analytical tools developed in this introduction and, with greater detail, in each of the essays, will highlight the value of thinking about the past when seeking to shape the present. Our aim is to help historians, social scientists, and practitioners assess with greater clarity the dynamics of international conflict management and global governance in the past and today.

## Connecting historical and social science research

Foreign intervention, global governance, and international conflict management have mostly been the domain of social scientists and legal scholars. Their studies primarily aim to develop generalizable definitions, concepts, and theories with which to assess and explain international conflicts and foreign intervention. These scholars have developed valuable theories and conceptual tools to make sense of global governance, including the latter’s “legitimacy gap” (Dingwerth et al. Citation 2019; Murray and Longo Citation 2018; Richmond and Mac Ginty Citation 2020b; Tallberg, Bäckstrand, and Scholte Citation 2018; Zürn Citation 2018), the pitfalls of humanitarian intervention (Coyne Citation 2013; Menon Citation 2016), and the advances and setbacks of the “responsibility to protect” (Bellamy Citation 2009; Chandler Citation 2004; de Waal Citation 2007; Ercan Citation 2022; Gilligan Citation 2013; Orford Citation 2011; Welsh Citation 2019). Most of these studies, however, are concerned with recent cases. If they discuss historical cases prior to 1989, they usually survey them in a cursory manner, based on textbooks and secondary sources.Footnote 1 Despite important exceptions (Nyers Citation 2006; Bass Citation 2013, Citation 2015), the overarching aims remain to survey large numbers of cases (Aydin Citation 2012; Berdal Citation 2008; Chesterman Citation 2001; Greig, Owsiak, and Diehl Citation 2019; MacQueen Citation 2011), to refine models (Finnemore Citation 2003; Holzgrefe Citation 2003; Pattison Citation 2010), and to advance normative arguments (Power Citation 2002; Seymour Citation 2012).

Meanwhile, in recent years, a growing number of historical studies have turned their attention to humanitarian intervention, development aid, United Nations peacekeeping operations, and past regimes of global governance.Footnote 2 These historical approaches are vital to the wider debate as most social science accounts tend to simplify past developments to either straightforward continuities or clear breaks at specific moments in time. Usually, they depict 1945 and 1989 as watershed moments for “modern” global governance and conflict management, ignoring recent historical research on the dynamics of the interwar years and the Cold War era.Footnote 3 Historical studies, by contrast, highlight the continuities and breaks as well as the often contradictory dynamics in the scope, narratives, and power constellations that make up global governance at different moments in time.

Yet historical studies have their blind spots, too, and can therefore benefit enormously from a more constructive engagement with social science literature. Many historical studies explore past conflicts without much concern for comparisons, concepts, or policy relevance. Historians are quick to discard studies by social scientists as lacking contextual nuance, and they routinely “deconstruct” culturally insensitive concepts and methodologies without offering alternative analytical frameworks. Historians rightfully allude to European colonial violence and Western liberal imperialism as historical roots of current human rights rhetoric, the “responsibility to protect”, and peacebuilding (Eckel Citation 2019, 354; Klose Citation 2022, 249–250; Mazower Citation 2009, 14–15; Rodogno Citation 2022, 316–317; Tudor Citation 2023, 10, 14; cf. for a more cautious view Muschik Citation 2022, 252). But they rarely follow up their critique by making concrete proposals on how we can use awareness of the past to change practices and concepts of global governance, conflict management, and foreign intervention in the present. At the end of her excellent recent study, Eva-Maria Muschik (Citation 2022, 254) makes an important plea for the need to establish local mechanisms of control of intervening forces, while the latter would need to live up to their enormous responsibility. Clearly, historians should make their voices heard more often and more effectively in the context of such discussions.

In the following, we make just such an attempt: to connect historical research with social science studies and explore ways to bring the insights of historical research to bear on current discussions among social scientists and practitioners in the fields of foreign intervention, conflict management, and global governance. Drawing on social science concepts and theories, we seek to develop definitions of key terms that are sensitive to shifting historical contexts. This conceptual rigour allows us to identify recurring patterns. Notably, we identify and explore several more general challenges interveners have faced across different settings. At the end of this introduction, we present and discuss some of the tentative historical lessons derived from our case studies. We hope that adding a currently missing historical dimension to the debates around foreign interventions, conflict management, and global governance will stimulate debate among policymakers, social scientists, and historians. We also hope that this effort will help make historical research more accessible to scholars in neighbouring fields and enrich empirical and theoretical work in the social sciences, where scholars are struggling to capture and “operationalize” complex historical dynamics.

## Defining foreign intervention, global governance, and “regimes” of conflict management

We define foreign intervention as a specific form of international conflict management, where external state or non-state actors cross territorial borders with the aim of influencing the outcome of a conflict or crisis in another sovereign state.Footnote 4 Foreign interventions, in other words, are substantial external intrusions into the domestic sovereignty of a state or a non-sovereign territory under the control of another state or stateless society, as in the case of the Gaza Strip. This wide definition includes interventions requested by the government of the affected state or relevant political authority and those carried out against its will, and it also includes interventions sanctioned by international law and those violating it. It covers a wide range of military, economic, and cultural activities, so long as these have a deliberate and significant impact on the affected state’s, or relevant political authority’s, capacity for autonomous action.

The wide scope of this definition does not mean that any cross-border action represents a case of foreign intervention. Instead, the definition distinguishes foreign interventions, on the one hand, from less intrusive forms of cross-border interaction, such as trade, cultural exchange, and regular diplomacy, which do not substantially infringe on the sovereignty of the affected state. On the other hand, it sets foreign interventions apart from outright wars of annexation and military aggression that primarily serve territorial motives. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, for instance, would fall outside our definition. For all we know – and despite the claim of Russian President Vladimir Putin that the invasion is not a war but a “special miliary operation” according to Chapter VII of the UN Charter – Russia’s attack is aimed not merely at regime change or primarily at the protection of minorities but at the annexation of large parts of Ukrainian territory and the transformation of Ukraine into a Russian vassal state.Footnote 5

In empirical and historical reality, of course, these distinctions between foreign intervention and milder cross-border activity, on the one hand, and outright war, on the other, are rarely clear cut. Our aim is not to propose a new definition of foreign interventions that helps neatly classify and code large samples of past conflicts and crises. Instead, our wider definition of foreign intervention aims to allow for the comparative historical analysis of diverse forms of intrusive cross-border action to manage conflicts and crises. It enables us to assess recurring dynamics and patterns of global conflict management across a variety of historical settings and to trace larger historical shifts in conflict management and global governance over time.

In view of the manifold historical mixtures of motives, justifications, and local dynamics of foreign interventions, we therefore deliberately refrain from narrow and clear-cut categories.Footnote 6 As our case studies demonstrate, irrespective of their legal or political classification, foreign interventions always contain a varying mixture of selfish motives of interveners, selfless public justifications, and often unexpected dynamics on the ground. As conceived here, then, foreign interventions can range from fiscal control and the implementation of social or cultural reforms to arbitration, peacekeeping, and military intervention (see also Greig, Owsiak, and Diehl Citation 2019, 6–10; Williams and Bellamy Citation 2021, 1). Foreign interventions can aim both at preventing the escalation (“managing”) of a conflict or crisis and at removing its root cause (“resolving” it).Footnote 7 They are always intrusive in nature and apply varying degrees of direct persuasion or coercion. In this sense, they differ from other forms of conflict management carried out without the direct involvement of foreign interveners, such as mediation and economic sanctions.Footnote 8 In contrast to wars, which serve primarily the aims of the warring parties, interveners justify foreign intervention with reference to the interests of the affected state, its population, and/or international peace and stability. Yet as interveners are primarily liable to their domestic audiences and the international community, they will inevitably pursue their own interests, too. As our historical cases and present-day instances of foreign intervention abundantly demonstrate, the interveners’ interests may overlap, but may also sharply conflict, with local needs.Footnote 9

As a form of cross-border action aimed at managing or resolving conflicts and crises, foreign interventions are a key tool of global governance. We define global governance here by its two principal functions: the exercise of political authority across state borders, as defined by Michael Zürn (Citation 2018, 3–4), and the cross-border coordination of policy to address global challenges, as defined by Thomas Weiss (Citation 2016, 227). Foreign interventions are not neutral and timeless tools, as some political science accounts seem to imply, but they result from a specific “regime” or historical era of global governance and conflict management that changes over time. While foreign interventions are enabled as well as bound by the norms, power structures, and practices of their time, their alleged “successes” or “failures” have repercussions on the regime of conflict management. The enormous financial and political costs of the UN intervention in Congo in the 1960s, ushering in a fifteen-year phase of relative stagnation in UN peacekeeping, is a case in point (see Claude Citation 1963; Muschik Citation 2022, 249; Williams and Bellamy Citation 2021, 59–60; and the contribution by Volker Prott to this special issue).

The scope, depth, and quality of global governance shift over time, giving rise to changing “regimes” or historical eras of global governance and conflict management. On the surface, a regime of conflict management is characterized by the existence and power of international law, international organizations, and intergovernmental or supranational coordinating structures such as the Concert of Europe in the nineteenth century or the European Union since the late twentieth century. A group of international relations scholars around Michael Zürn (Citation 2018, 111) has recently developed an index to measure the “cumulative authority” of international organizations since the end of World War I.Footnote 10 They found sharp rises after World War II and the end of the Cold War, gradual growth from about 1960 to 1975, and stagnation for most of the interwar years, the 1950s, and the final fifteen years of the Cold War. Yet while such quantitative assessments are useful as broad indicators of historical trends, we should be careful not to mistake the number of international organizations or changes in legal texts for the “reality” of global governance at a certain point in time (Barnett Citation 2021). Instead, we need closer historical scrutiny to examine the central qualitative features of a given global “regime” and assess how it operates in practice. These features include hierarchies within the system, but also its norms, informal rules, and conceptual underpinnings, ranging from the right of conquest, alleged “civilizing missions”, and mandates to shifting notions and constellations of development, culture, “race”, human rights, state sovereignty, minority protection, and self-determination. A useful label for this qualitative dimension of global governance is Williams and Bellamy’s (Citation 2021, 2) “codes of conduct” or Weiss’s (Citation 2016, 227) definition of global governance discussed above.

When tracing such broader trends of global governance over time, historical analysis not only reveals its “deepening” or (temporary) “decline” (Zürn Citation 2018, 3), but it scrutinizes continuities, breaks, and crises as well as overlaps and contradictions within and between eras or regimes of conflict management. It is important to qualify and indeed question schematic classifications of “strong paternalism” and “weak liberalism” before 1918 and “weak paternalism” and “strong liberalism” thereafter, as has been suggested by Michael Barnett (Citation 2012, 503–504, 510). While it is helpful to use analytical concepts like paternalism to explore changes and continuities of global governance over time, the underlying historical narrative, in this case, is based on the tacit claim that there was a clear break in the style of foreign domination after World War I – installing an institutionalized and more benign liberal internationalism and leaving behind the more violent, less liberal, and more paternalist colonial past.Footnote 11 Closer historical analysis demonstrates that notwithstanding larger trends towards more liberal and less paternalist rule across the twentieth century as a whole, the modes of foreign intervention and foreign domination have not changed in such a straightforward manner. How else could we account for the extreme violence meted out by European imperial powers against anti-colonial movements in Algeria or Kenya after World War II, or, for that matter, the growing criticism of violent colonial rule at the turn of the nineteenth to the twentieth century?

To elucidate this tension between historical ruptures and recurring patterns of foreign intervention, the history of international law is particularly useful (see Chesterman Citation 2001; Klose Citation 2017, Citation 2022, 237–250; Moyn Citation 2010, ch. 5). It underlines the dramatic transformations that contemporary views of the legality and legitimacy of foreign intervention underwent between the 1920s and the 1970s. The idea of connecting the protection of minorities – and, after 1945, the protection of human rights – with military intervention gained momentum among international lawyers during the 1920s and 1930s, reaching a peak in the face of the horrors of the Holocaust and World War II (Klose Citation 2017, 171). The following first phase of the Cold War from the late 1940s until the mid-1960s was characterized by a malleable framework of intervention. During this period, while non-intervention remained the legal norm, in practice, the UN Security Council authorized a significant number of foreign interventions and peacekeeping operations to contain Cold War tensions and manage decolonization, as happened in Kashmir, Korea, the Middle East, Congo, Cyprus, and other regions (Muschik Citation 2022; Tudor Citation 2023). From the mid-1960s, however, despite the work of prominent advocates of the legality of humanitarian interventions such as Hersch Lauterpacht and Richard B. Lillich and the rise of human rights activism in the West from the late 1970s, most international lawyers and legal advisors of governments and international organizations had settled on state sovereignty, and not human rights protection, as the primary and inviolable basis of international law (Moyn Citation 2010, 214–220).

These shifting legal conceptions mirrored but also directly affected the prevalence and forms of foreign intervention. Just as the more fluid early Cold War regime of conflict management tended to allow and, in some cases, facilitate overt UN intervention and peacekeeping missions, the increasing emphasis on state sovereignty and non-interference from the mid-1960s encouraged covert and unilateral military interventions as a resolution of crises and conflicts, as happened not only in East Pakistan in 1971, but also in Cambodia and Uganda in 1978–1979 – incidents “vigorously” and controversially discussed by contemporary legal scholars (Klose Citation 2022, 247).

For the purpose of this special issue, we approach international law as a volatile discursive and normative framework within – and oftentimes beyond and beneath – which politicians, diplomats, legal experts, humanitarian activists, mercenaries, scientific advisors, and others involved in foreign interventions planned, justified, and carried out their actions. Contemporary legal debates and norms reflect, and themselves inform, a specific historical regime of conflict management. Overall, our case studies underline the crucial impact that contemporary legal norms and the given regime of conflict management more generally had on the course of conflicts and crises. These “rules of the game” not merely informed interveners’ justifications and public statements, but they shaped the choice of the means, forms, and extent of interventions. Rather than simply authorizing or banning interventions, we find that a given historical regime of conflict management facilitated specific forms of interventions – at times limiting their scope, at times extending it, and, while producing some broader trends and recurring patterns, doing so hardly in a linear, straightforward fashion.

## Success and failure of foreign interventions and conflict management

A crucial part of a closer engagement with the contradictions and incongruities of conflict management and foreign interventions is to develop a benchmark for success and failure that reflects the empirical complexity and the historical dynamics involved. We examine the “success” and wider impact of past foreign interventions along four key dimensions. First, we investigate their direct impact on the region or state affected, including its population. Here, context-specific historical research based on the study of primary documents allows us to look inside what is often a “black box”. We reconstruct those regions affected by outside interference as dynamic settings of transnational encounters that at the same time transform local structures and shape the course of the foreign intervention, likely with repercussions on the international system and its “regime” of global governance and conflict management. Second, we assess to what extent a foreign intervention serves the interests of the intervener, which may be states or international organizations or non-state actors. Here, it is important to distinguish between the publicly declared aims of the intervention and the not publicly visible, often strategic rationales that motivate interveners' actions. Again, historical research has the benefit of allowing us to access classified documents that provide insights into the covert dimensions of foreign interventions. Third, and crucial for international organizations, we assess the impact of foreign interventions on the international system. Were they successful in localizing conflicts and preventing a possible threat to wider international peace and stability?

Finally, we suggest adding a fourth, historical dimension to measuring the success of foreign interventions. “Success” and “failure” are time specific. Foreign interventions and their aims are defined by the norms, mindsets, hierarchies, and policy tools available at a given moment in time. Partition, for instance, may have seemed inevitable or even desirable in the mid-twentieth century, because it corresponded to the ideal of clear-cut and homogeneous national units ensuring international stability. In the twenty-first century, in turn, partition seems to most observers neither desirable nor inevitable, because international norms have changed in favour of an emphasis on minority rights, multi-level governance, and democratic power sharing. When assessing foreign interventions, we should therefore also focus on their relationship to the overarching regime of global governance and conflict management: to what extent did the foreign intervention in question result from that era’s regime of conflict management? Did it serve to strengthen and vindicate this regime, or did it rather undermine (parts of) it? This fourth dimension of “success” thus allows us to assess foreign interventions before the background of their time, and it opens the view to broader changes in the norms, values, and practices that constitute global governance.

## Challenges for interveners and conflict managers

As our historical case studies show, when external interveners cross a border to influence the course and outcome of a conflict or crisis, regardless of their specific mandate or aims, they meet several recurring challenges. At the most basic level, this concerns a lack of funds or troops.Footnote 12 In China after World War II, the UNESCO mission was unable to raise more financial support from either the Chinese government, which faced hyperinflation and focused on the civil war, or the American government or international organizations or NGOs. Ultimately, operating on a small budget, UNESCO had to rely on the support of local Chinese educational activist groups, which proved to be insufficient for the highly ambitious liberal project to have sustained influence in China. In the Congo Crisis a decade later, which saw the largest military UN intervention of the Cold War, the UN was brought to the brink of financial collapse and finally forced to withdraw after four years of a mission that had assumed the proportions of a post-colonial nation-building exercise. But the country was far from stabilized: only weeks after the UN had withdrawn the bulk of its forces and declared the success of its mission, a ferocious civil war broke out that ended in the victory of the US-backed regime of Colonel Mobutu, ushering in more than three decades of dictatorial rule and economic stagnation.

Another common practical challenge is the understanding of local conditions (see also Pouligny Citation 2005, Citation 2006; Autesserre Citation 2019). In Austria after World War I, League of Nations officials, while they had some local knowledge, preferred to rely on their neoliberal doctrines of balanced budgets and cuts to the public sector in their attempt to reconstruct the country’s economy. In their centralizing zeal, moreover, they ignored the federal structure of the country, where the regions traditionally had a strong influence on financial policies. Crucially, League officials failed to take up grassroots-level initiatives and local calls for boosting investment to stimulate economic growth. Relying on a strong central government and a top-down doctrine of textbook financial reform, the League’s measures undermined their own legitimacy with the population and proved to be largely counterproductive. Instead of reconstructing and modernizing the Austrian economy, the League had deepened social divisions in the country, undercut the credibility of the international community, and thus contributed to political polarization and defiance among many Austrians of the new international order. Similarly, in Congo, many of the UN troops and civilian officials not only had little knowledge of the country and its history, but many of them did not speak French, which meant that they were unable to communicate with most local politicians and people. In the small territory of the Gaza Strip, UN peacekeepers also failed to respond to local circumstances, instead increasing inequalities and insecurities in the already confined and militarized borderland.

In many of the conflicts and crises we have examined, different intervening powers and groups competed for influence, sometimes pursuing diametrically opposed aims. In East Pakistan in 1971, for instance, the allegedly non-political and purely humanitarian aid provided by the UN through the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to both India and Pakistan was directly challenged by radical humanitarian organizations who attempted to illegally cross the border of East Pakistan and deliver aid directly to the people. Using arguments reminiscent of the later concept of the “responsibility to protect”, these “rogue” humanitarian activists refused to accept Pakistani state sovereignty in the face of the regime’s assault on its East Bengali population. Meanwhile, India clandestinely trained and armed the East Bengali rebel force to fight government troops in East Pakistan. In its desire to gain a foothold in Vietnam in the 1970s, UNHCR came to obstruct its own mission of protecting refugees, whose presence caused friction not only with the Vietnamese government, but also with major donor states, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom.

In addition to these practical challenges, the intervening powers were also impeded by limitations resulting from their own internal organizational structures and the fact that their main donors and audiences lay outside of the territory affected by the intervention.Footnote 13 The lack of control local people and governments had over the measures of the interveners was often the direct result of the latter’s top-down approach. In the case of Austria, as we have seen above, League of Nations officials followed their own doctrine and were hardly open to local initiatives. In Kashmir after 1947, the UN first sought to resolve the territorial dispute by a plebiscite. When this did not seem to work, some increasingly frustrated UN advisors and US policymakers suggested partition of the region along a border defined by experts – revealing the endurance of colonial mindsets in Western circles beyond the independence of India and Pakistan.

Another issue arising from the structural mismatch between the interveners’ and the locals’ interests is the former’s lack of legitimacy in the eyes of local politicians and communities. In Austria, this lack of legitimacy of the League of Nations’ measures was a major impediment for the effectiveness of the economic and financial reforms. In Congo, the UN positioned itself in opposition to the democratically elected Congolese government of Patrice Lumumba. Despite pledging impartiality and a diplomatic approach, UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld was reluctant to accept African agency in the definition and solution of the crisis. The main reason why the UN failed in Kashmir, in turn, was arguably its lack of credibility as an effective and legitimate mediator among the different interested parties. After the fall of Saigon in 1975, to give another example, UNHCR sought to gain the trust of the communist unified government in Vietnam and expand its reach to the communist world. To win the sympathies of the Vietnamese government, which did not want to be branded as a violent regime producing political refugees, and conscious of the unwillingness of Western states to accept more refugees, UNHCR actively worked to prevent refugees from leaving Vietnam. The organization thus cynically used refugees to pursue its wider geostrategic ambitions and violated its own original mandate, which is to protect and assist refugees.

Bureaucratic self-interest is another recurring obstacle for interveners, specifically for international organizations such as the League of Nations and the UN. As non-democratic institutions that depend on private donations and/or state funding, over time, many of these organizations develop a specific internal culture and aims that focus on the survival and expansion of the organization rather than merely the pursuit of their original agenda (see also Barnett and Finnemore Citation 2004; Dingwerth et al. Citation 2019). Thus, in the case of East Pakistan in 1971, UNHCR officials shied away from making any public comments about the political causes or a political solution to the refugee crisis, focusing their energies ostensibly on the humanitarian side of the situation. At the same time, the ambitious UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadruddin Aga Khan, sought to use the crisis to expand the scope of his UN agency to become a global political actor (on Sadruddin Khan see Loescher Citation 2001, ch. 6; Myard Citation 2010). Something similar happened in Vietnam, where Sadruddin Khan’s ambitions to expand UNHCR’s global reach resulted in the agency’s reluctance to intervene in refugee-like situations, despite the High Commissioner’s mandate to protect refugees. Paradoxically, the organization only succeeded in expanding its influence and size when it, under the new leadership of Poul Hartling, resumed its core task of refugee protection in 1979 through the installation of the Orderly Departure Program for Refugees from Vietnam.

Next to practical and organizational challenges, interveners also face major political obstacles. Most importantly, of course, interveners are inevitably forced to grapple with the diverging strategic interests of the states involved as well as the dominant norm of non-interference in the domestic affairs of other states. In some cases, like East Pakistan, the norm of non-interference and Cold War politics outright prevented any overt form of foreign intervention beyond the delivery of humanitarian aid. In other cases, notably in Austria and Congo, the large-scale presence of an external power guiding or directly dictating policy choices, even if formally authorized, undermined fragile democratic structures that had followed imperial and colonial rule, respectively. Particularly in Congo, strategic manoeuvring by European (post-)colonial powers Belgium and Britain, but also by the United States, further complicated the UN’s attempt to achieve a durable resolution to the conflict. In post-World War II China, rising Cold War tensions politicized UNESCO’s educational project, associating the Chinese nationalist government in the eyes of many local people with negative foreign influence and lending further credence to the communists who portrayed themselves as defenders of Chinese interests. The establishment of the new government in Beijing and the relocation of the nationalist government to Taiwan and the Western support of the latter as the official Chinese government with a seat in the UN eliminated any possibility of delivering UNESCO projects in mainland China. Another example of how Western strategic priorities hampered efforts to address a specific regional crisis is the UN peacekeeping operation in the Middle East, which partly resulted from, and was shaped by, the Western European oil supply crisis following the Suez Crisis in 1956.

## Overcoming and circumventing the challenges

The seven cases of international conflict management explored in this special issue indicate that League of Nations and United Nations officials generally sought to meet practical challenges by adapting their approach to local conditions. In Congo, the UN quickly realized the need for its officers and civilian advisors not only to have at least a basic knowledge of French but also some knowledge of the wider African context. To alleviate the lack of local knowledge and boost the UN’s credibility and reduce its dependence on the United States and former European colonial powers, they began recruiting more French-speaking staff, while most troops came from neutral European countries like Sweden and Ireland, other African countries, and India. Dag Hammarskjöld and his successor, U Thant, also successfully bid for more financial support and troops from UN member states to address funding shortages. In China, UNESCO began working with a prominent local missionary who had extensive knowledge of the Chinese context to help improve the effectiveness of its measures. In East Pakistan, UNHCR centralized and coordinated humanitarian efforts to increase efficiency, reduce competition among charities, and ensure a clear channel of communication with the governments of India and Pakistan. In the Gaza Strip, Egypt, which had governed the area through a governor-general from 1948 onwards, came to the rescue of the UN by setting up a series of economic and political initiatives to address both pre-existing problems and the problems created by the presence of the UN’s peacekeeping operation.

Yet our research also reveals that the same international interveners in some instances responded to obstacles by circumventing legal and political limitations, venturing into legal grey zones, and redefining their aims and what a “successful” intervention would look like. In the refugee crises in Vietnam in the second half of the 1970s, UNHCR redefined who counted as a “refugee” and began negotiating directly with the different political factions to sidestep legal and political limitations that would have prevented them from becoming involved as a significant humanitarian and political force in the conflict. In Congo a decade earlier, the UN under Dag Hammarskjöld reinterpreted Security Council resolutions in open disagreement with the Lumumba administration to justify a much more ambitious mission that aimed to establish the UN as the sole mediator and the de facto supreme military and political authority in the country. League of Nations officials operating in interwar Austria similarly readjusted their ambitious aim of post-war economic reconstruction to technical targets of balanced budgets, obtaining loans, or establishing a central bank, ignoring the wider economic and political costs of their measures.

The cases surveyed in this special issue demonstrate, moreover, that the discrepancy between the interveners’ often extensive mandate to secure peace and stability and prevent mass human rights abuses, on the one hand, and their limited legal and political authority, on the other, incentivized them to pursue their political and strategic aims covertly, usually under the cloak of “impartial” technical and humanitarian rhetoric.Footnote 14 While using the allegedly neutral language of balanced budgets and fiscal reform, what the League of Nations really aimed at in post-war Austria was to prop the country up as a “civilized” bulwark and a cornerstone of the post-war international order established at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919. In a similar vein, UNESCO’s efforts in China were phased out by the Chinese communist government, suspecting UNESCO to pursue Western liberal interests. Using high-flying legal and moral rhetoric to pledge impartiality, Dag Hammarskjöld’s policies in Congo were driven by wider strategic aims: to preserve the territorial integrity of the state and thus bolster the principle of national sovereignty against the right of self-determination; to confront radical African nationalism with its pan-African, non-aligned, and secessionist leanings; and to assign the former colony its place in an international hierarchy dominated by the great powers and managed by the UN. Similarly, in East Pakistan, UNHCR used humanitarian aid and support of the refugees as an entry point for covertly pursuing its conservative political aim, which amounted to a return to the status quo ante.

Challenges and failures, finally, prompted League of Nations and United Nations officials to adjust their overall strategy in order to survive as an organization and political force in a changing regime of global governance and conflict management. Following the mixed successes and setbacks of its economic intervention in Austria, the League of Nations used an adapted model in Hungary and with the Dawes Plan in Germany in 1924. The inability of the UN to carry out a plebiscite and broker a solution in Kashmir led not only to frustration but also to less ambitious and more pragmatic assessments of what UN soft power could achieve in difficult territorial disputes. As the UN mission in the Middle East indicates, “peacekeeping” in the sense of conflict management and stabilization rather than conflict resolution was one such consequence. The Congo Crisis a few years later was a major turning point not just for the UN but also for global governance more generally. Having overstretched its political, economic, and moral authority and acting in a cooling international climate of détente and relative stability, the UN henceforth adopted a much more cautious stance towards conflict management. A direct result was the restrained approach of U Thant in the East Pakistan crisis of 1971, which the UN secretary-general depicted as a humanitarian tragedy rather than a case of self-determination and mass human rights abuses that required strong international action.

One important way to adapt to the multiple challenges of conflict management, particularly for international organizations, was, and still is, to retreat to a technical and humanitarian definition of aims and measures.Footnote 15 In the case of UNHCR in East Pakistan and Vietnam in the 1970s, this publicly depoliticized approach allowed the organization to circumvent the barrier of state sovereignty while at the same time shielding it from allegations of political interference or even failure when a conflict escalated (on depoliticization see Maertens and Louis Citation 2021). While this approach has transformed UNHCR into the single largest UN agency and a major global humanitarian organization, it has also meant that the organization has acted in direct opposition to the interests of refugees (see also Barnett and Finnemore Citation 2004, ch. 4). In a wider perspective, the risk of the “safe” option of portraying the UN and international organizations merely as extended relief agencies is to leave political conflict management to state power and an anarchical (or at best highly hierarchical) international system. The recent crises in Ukraine and the Middle East have revealed the enormous risks of such a state-driven regime of international conflict management with a weak United Nations remaining on the sidelines.

## The “success” and wider impact of foreign interventions and conflict management

The historical cases reviewed here demonstrate how foreign interventions and international conflict management have gone through recurring cycles of high aspirations, followed by frustration, retreat, and readjustment. Our research illustrates that even when some achievements are made, there are enormous dangers in conflict management gone wrong. The destructive potential of failed conflict management includes exacerbating economic difficulties and political polarization (Austria in the 1920s); aggravating a domestic struggle for power and international recognition and discrediting the liberal option (UNESCO in post-World War II China); the entrenchment of territorial disputes to seemingly irresolvable national antagonisms (Kashmir); the creation of self-perpetuating conflicts and peacekeeping economies (the Middle East); the establishment of puppet regimes and failed states (Congo); and the rise of the “undemocratic liberalism” of international bureaucracies that betray their original mission merely to expand in size and authority (UNHCR in Vietnam and East Pakistan).Footnote 16

As outlined above, we assess the impact of foreign interventions and international conflict management along four key dimensions: (i) their local and regional impact, (ii) whether they served the interests of the interveners, (iii) their repercussions on the international system, and (iv) the extent to which they altered the “regime” of conflict management and the “rules of the game” of global governance. At the local and regional levels, our research demonstrates that foreign intervention can indeed have positive effects. The League of Nations’ attempts to assist in the economic reconstruction of Austria in the 1920s stabilized the country’s currency and obtained vital foreign loans. In Kashmir after 1947, despite the setbacks, the UN presence prevented an all-out Indo-Pakistani war and created a forum for bilateral negotiations. In its short lifespan, the UNESCO project in post-war China delivered some concrete benefits for the local population, educating them about public health measures and delivering medical examinations and vaccinations. In a systemic perspective that ignores Palestinian realities, the presence of a large UN force internationalized the tense and potentially violent Egyptian–Israeli relationship, thereby reducing the risk of a return to warfare. In the Congo Crisis of the early 1960s, the UN was initially successful in putting a stop to Belgian military and economic interference and in securing the territorial integrity of the country. Even for East Pakistan, where conflict management was limited to overt humanitarian aid and conflicting covert attempts to enforce a solution to the crisis, one might conclude that the rigid Cold War order at least prevented a wider or even global escalation of the conflict. And UNHCR’s efforts in Vietnam in the 1970s, finally, provided relief and security to a significant number of refugees.

Even so, upon closer inspection, on the same local and regional level, the record of foreign interventions in our cases is overall rather mixed. Austria saw political stability and public service undermined by the League of Nations’ emphasis on balanced budgets and their top-down decision-making, impeding both the economic and the political consolidation of the new republic. The failure to broker a solution in Kashmir resulted in a military and political stalemate between India and Pakistan that entrenched the two states’ rivalry and continues unresolved to this day, not to speak of the dire situation for the people living in the area. In China, UNESCO was ill-equipped to bring its ambitious education programme to fruition as it was forced to operate on a small budget and act within Cold War constraints and a civil war context. In the Middle East, the UN presence generated both insecurities and “peacekeeping economies” that caused long-term dependence on foreign aid rather than bringing any stability to the Gaza Strip. Acting in the style of a neo-colonial power, UN troops and administrators in Congo undermined the authority of the elected government of Patrice Lumumba. As the UN did not have the means to effectively train the Congolese military, build infrastructure, or set up a broad network of schools – in other words, to durably “develop” Congo into a self-sustaining, stable polity – the UN’s increasingly aggressive military operations fuelled violence and insecurity while making stability dependent on the presence of a large UN force. The East Pakistan crisis is perhaps the most blatant failure of international conflict management among our cases as it was ultimately resolved by unilateral Indian military intervention. UNHCR’s Orderly Departure Programme for Refugees from Vietnam, which allowed for the resettlement of hundreds of thousands of Indochinese from 1979 onwards, is often hailed as a successful humanitarian intervention in the Cold War framework. Yet it left its executors with the uneasy feeling that they, as UN officials, had violated a basic human right, namely the right of any person to leave their country (Kumin Citation 2008).

Our cases demonstrate that for the interveners, conflict management holds numerous benefits. In moments of rapid shifts of the international order, as happened after the two world wars, at the peak of the anti-colonial movement in the early 1960s, or in the immediate aftermath of the Cold War, structures and norms of international politics become malleable. Interveners can seek to exploit such moments to expand the scope and size of their organization. The League of Nations in Austria in the 1920s, the young United Nations in Kashmir in the late 1940s, or UN troops in Congo in the early 1960s: these more assertive overt forms of foreign intervention to reconstruct economies, resolve major international disputes, or end European post-colonial interference and keep the Cold War out of Africa were made possible in the context of fundamental changes in the “regime” of global governance and conflict management. As the example of UNHCR since the early 1970s demonstrates, moreover, interveners can also gradually grow by adopting a more conservative approach of seeking to work within and stabilize the international system and playing by the rules of (overt) non-interference and impartiality.

However, failed intervention and conflict management also bear the risk of damaging the interveners’ reputation and influence. The failure of the League of Nations to prevent the growing military aggressions of the 1930s and the war ultimately sealed its fate. Following the debacle in Congo, the United Nations was forced to abandon Dag Hammarskjöld’s expansive agenda of proactive peacekeeping. The failures of the UN in Somalia in 1993 and in Rwanda and Bosnia in the two following years had a similarly devastating effect not only on the organization’s credibility but also on its willingness and ability to focus on the resolution of international crises. If an intervener or “conflict manager” such as UNHCR grows to the detriment of its original mission and becomes dysfunctional, it risks not only widespread criticism but, in the long run, also jeopardizing funding and state support.

The course and outcome of individual cases of conflict management and foreign intervention can therefore have significant repercussions on the international order and the wider “regime” of global governance and conflict management, our third measure of “success”. As we have seen, certain dynamics and tendencies of foreign interventions such as a top-down approach, the exploitation of legal grey zones, and the covert pursuit of external strategic aims can weaken local social and political structures. As a result, fragile democratic regimes may crumble under political polarization, civil war, or military coups. The consequences for the international system can be severe. The erosion of domestic stability can be accompanied by or lead to violent irredentism and external aggression. A weakened Austria was unable to withstand the assault of Nazi Germany in 1938, the latter itself emboldened by what the Nazi regime perceived to be a weak and illegitimate international order. In other cases, failed conflict resolution can create entrenched and seemingly irresolvable conflicts as in Kashmir and the Middle East. The ongoing crisis in Syria is a stark reminder of how a local conflict can threaten wider peace and security and the fabric of the international order – when Russia used the conflict as a military rehearsal for its current invasion of Ukraine (see Marnam Citation 2022) while Turkey, Russia, and Belarus have used Syrian refugees as leverage to exert pressure on the European Union (see Greenhill Citation 2022; Lupieri Citation 2021). Likewise, the military dictatorships and economic stagnation that followed European colonial rule and subsequent foreign interventions notably in Africa and the Middle East have not only had devastating effects on the affected populations, but also contributed to increasing global economic disparities and prepared the ground for the rise of radical movements that violently challenge the international order.

The symbolic level matters, too. Failures like the League of Nations efforts in Austria and the UN’s unsuccessful attempts to resolve the conflicts in Kashmir, the Middle East, and Congo weaken the public’s and political leaders’ trust in these international organizations as legitimate and effective actors to turn to for resolving conflicts and expressing grievances. The result may be a pervading sense that international and multilateral conflict management is as useless and ineffective as it is illegitimate, if not outright dangerous. Such perceptions, if they take hold among global publics and their leaders, may reinforce notions of, and reliance on, the “traditional” actors and tools of international politics: strong states pursuing their strategic interests in an “anarchical” system stabilized by clear hierarchies of power and strong state borders. In such a system, international law, NGOs, and international organizations are tasked with alleviating the “collateral damage” of crises and conflicts rather than playing an active role in their prevention and resolution. This division of labour – with states “resolving” conflicts and international organizations taking care of the humanitarian fallout – may be stable for some time and have the additional “benefit” of reducing accountability for states and risks for non-state actors. Yet in an ever more globalized and interdependent world, the rigid hierarchies and unpredictable nature of such a system are bound to produce periodic crises and conflicts that have the potential to cause the entire order to collapse. The wars and conflicts of the twentieth century are stark reminders of the inherent risks of international systems with weak “regimes” of international conflict management and strong reliance on state power and international hierarchies.

## Historical lessons and reflection points

We want to conclude by offering several lessons from history or, more modestly, “reflection points” that emerge from our analysis of twentieth-century cases of League of Nations and United Nations intervention and conflict management. Some of these points confirm suggestions that have been made by social scientists, others may run counter to such suggestions, and yet others might likely be dismissed as unrealistic. Even so, our aim here is to bring historical insights to bear on the current debate and stimulate further discussion and reflection.

First, we need to find ways to make interveners directly accountable to the populations affected by their action. Drawing on Barnett’s (Citation 2012) important insight that every foreign intervention has an inherent element of paternalism and power difference, it is important that interveners not only formulate clear aims for their actions but that these actions are bound to the interests of the local population. Improving and enforcing local accountability in foreign intervention, although difficult to achieve in practice (Richmond and Mac Ginty Citation 2020a, 2–3; Tallberg, Bäckstrand, and Scholte Citation 2018), seems to be the only effective mechanism to prevent abuse of power and interventions that serve the interests of the interveners and the international system rather than the people affected.Footnote 17

Second, international humanitarian action needs to be repoliticized. Our case studies demonstrate that the division between political conflict resolution, usually left to states, and humanitarian aid provision, carried out by UN agencies or NGOs, serves primarily the interests of the various interveners and the maintenance of international hierarchies. It liberates those interveners, usually the UN and NGOs, who provide aid and their “good offices”, from the charge of taking sides and from assuming responsibility for the political solution of a crisis or conflict. At the same time, separating the political from the humanitarian aspects of foreign intervention opens grey zones for the “humanitarian” interveners through which they might seek to pursue tacit political aims under the cloak of impartiality and administrative and technical aid. Therefore, all types of foreign interventions need to formulate clear political strategies alongside humanitarian and other objectives.Footnote 18 We contend that the recommendation to depoliticize humanitarian aid and decouple it from political rationales, as recently proposed by Tateyama (Citation 2018, 119), is counterproductive.

Third, we need to strengthen and democratize the main structures of the United Nations. For global governance to work, it needs to be both legitimate and effective. To overcome deadlock in the Security Council while at the same time increasing democratic control and reducing hierarchies within the UN, we would suggest abolishing both the right of veto and the existence of permanent seats in the Security Council. It is true that the veto is an important mechanism to keep the great powers within the UN structure and, in some sense, an advance compared to its predecessor, the League of Nations (Mazower Citation 2009, 16). Even so, together with permanent membership, the veto effectively paralyses the UN in the most dangerous international crises. If, however, the UN Security Council or a similar executive organ were elected by the members of the General Assembly for a limited period of time, it would gain in legitimacy and, in turn, in effectiveness, possibly balancing the loss of the veto and permanent membership and taking steps that might prevent a collapse of the international order and lead us out of the present crisis.

## Abstract

The introduction places the essays in this special issue in the context of recent studies by social scientists and historians on foreign interventions, international conflict management, and global governance. It defines the key terms used in the case studies and discusses the various dimensions of what constitutes “success” in foreign interventions carried out by international organizations in post-imperial/post-colonial contexts. The introduction then assesses the seven case studies examined in the five essays in this special issue. These span the period from the early 1920s to the late 1970s, cover parts of Europe, the Middle East, central Africa, and Asia, and range from financial reconstruction and fundamental education programmes to refugee resettlement, peacekeeping, and military intervention. Despite the large variety of historical contexts and forms of intervention, the introduction identifies several common challenges that League of Nations and United Nations officials faced as they sought to influence the outcome of a domestic crisis or conflict. These challenges include not only practical issues such as lack of local knowledge or budgetary constraints, but also the persistence of patronizing attitudes, secrecy, competition with other external interveners, and, crucially, a mismatch between the interests of the international interveners and the populations affected. The introduction then assesses the main strategies the League of Nations and United Nations interveners used to overcome these challenges. It demonstrates that they frequently overstepped their mandates, ventured into legal grey zones, adopted covert strategies of intervention, or avoided meaningful action while settling on safer and allegedly apolitical and “impartial” humanitarian aid. The final section discusses the mixed historical record of foreign interventions and international conflict management and the severe risks both of failure and of inaction. It concludes by offering some tentative historical “lessons” or reflection points that may stimulate current debates among social scientists and practitioners working in international organizations.
