[When the Falconets Took England Apart: Nigeria’s 3–0 Masterclass in Bielsko-Biała By Jide Adesina | 1stAfrika.com There are football victories that arrive quietly, recorded in the statistics and quickly forgotten. Then there are victories that announce themselves with the force of a national statement. Nigeria’s 3–0 demolition of England in the Round of 16 of the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland belonged firmly to the second category. On Thursday afternoon in Bielsko-Biała, the Falconets did not merely survive a knockout contest. They walked into the Stadion Miejski with the authority of a team that had decided that England would not be allowed to write the next chapter of Nigeria’s World Cup story. And by the time the final whistle came, Nigeria had written it themselves. The scoreboard was brutally simple: England 0, Nigeria 3. Tosin Rafiu had struck early. Seimeyeha Janet Akekoromowei had doubled the advantage almost immediately after halftime. Mary Mamudu had delivered the final blow in the 73rd minute. Between those goals stood another story altogether: a goalkeeper who refused to surrender, a defence that absorbed pressure, a midfield that repeatedly disrupted England’s rhythm, and an attack that punished every opening. ￼ The stadium had barely settled into the afternoon when Nigeria delivered its first warning. Eight minutes were on the clock when Rafiu turned an English mistake into Nigerian opportunity. She intercepted a loose pass high up the pitch, accelerated into the penalty area and, from an increasingly difficult angle, found the finish that sent the ball beyond Katie Cox. It was not simply an early goal. It changed the psychological landscape of the match. England had entered the knockout stage knowing that one mistake could be fatal. Nigeria immediately demonstrated why. The Falconets were not going to wait patiently for England to establish control. They were going to attack the spaces, challenge the English defenders and force the Young Lionesses to play under pressure. England responded. That response is important because the 3–0 scoreline should not obscure what happened in the opening half. England created opportunities and, for stretches, threatened seriously. Princess Ademiluyi found space, Lily Dent pushed forward and Rachel Maltby became increasingly involved. Nigeria’s defence was being tested, and this was where Christiana Uzoma began to write her own chapter of the afternoon. The Nigerian goalkeeper was magnificent. She was not simply a spectator behind a defence protecting a one-goal advantage. She was repeatedly required to rescue it. One of her most important interventions came when Ademiluyi found herself with a clear opportunity. Uzoma stood her ground and made the save. Another English attack followed, and again Uzoma was there. Then came the moment that could have transformed the entire contest. England won a penalty after a lengthy VAR review following a foul on Ademiluyi. Rachel Maltby stood over the ball with Nigeria’s early advantage suddenly under direct threat. The stadium waited. Maltby struck. Uzoma reacted. The Nigerian goalkeeper got enough on the penalty to push it onto the crossbar, preserving Nigeria’s 1–0 lead. ￼ That save was more than a goalkeeping statistic. It was the emotional hinge of the match. Had England equalised before halftime, the entire complexion of the contest could have changed. Instead, Nigeria walked into the dressing room still ahead. The Falconets had survived England’s best first-half examination. But survival was never going to be enough. When Nigeria emerged for the second half, they returned with the urgency of a team determined to settle the argument. Two minutes after the restart, the English defence failed to properly clear a corner. The ball remained alive inside the danger area and Akekoromowei reacted with devastating precision. She struck. The ball found the net. Nigeria 2, England 0. Suddenly England were no longer chasing an equaliser. They were chasing a way back into a match that Nigeria was beginning to own. ￼ The second goal revealed another quality in this Nigerian side: ruthlessness. The Falconets did not need to dominate possession every second. They understood where the match could be won. They pressed when England were vulnerable, defended when England attacked and moved forward with purpose when the opportunity appeared. England tried to respond with substitutions and increased attacking pressure. But Nigeria’s structure remained remarkably difficult to break. And then came the third. The clock moved into the 73rd minute when Akekoromowei again became central to the attack. She won the ball near the byline after England struggled to deal with the situation and squared it into the danger area. Mary Mamudu had entered the match as a substitute in the 61st minute. Twelve minutes later, she delivered the decisive moment. Mamudu met the opportunity and finished into an unguarded net. Nigeria 3, England 0. The English resistance had been broken. The Falconets now had something far more valuable than a lead. They had control of the match. England continued to push, but Nigeria’s defenders had learned the rhythm of the opposition. Attempts were blocked. Attacks were disrupted. England were repeatedly caught offside, and when they did manage to find a path toward goal, Uzoma and the Nigerian defence stood between them and redemption. ￼ The closing stages became a demonstration of Nigerian composure. Moses Aduku used his bench intelligently, bringing on fresh legs to maintain the intensity and protect the advantage. Victory Lucky, Winner Onajite David and Folajomi Olabiyi entered as Nigeria managed the final stages. There was no panic. No desperate retreat. No collapse under pressure. Nigeria played like a team that understood exactly what the scoreboard meant and exactly what was required to get to the quarter-finals. When the referee finally ended the contest, the Nigerian players could celebrate what they had accomplished. England had been eliminated. Nigeria had advanced. And the manner of the victory made it particularly significant. The Falconets had not reached the quarter-finals through a narrow escape or a penalty shootout. They had defeated England by three clear goals while keeping a clean sheet. The result also represented the biggest World Cup victory in a meeting between Nigeria and England across their men’s and women’s senior and U-20 teams, according to reporting from ACLSports. ￼ For Nigeria, the victory also continued a remarkable scoring run. After four matches, the Falconets had scored 13 goals in the tournament. ￼ But numbers alone cannot explain what happened in Bielsko-Biała. This was a performance built around moments of courage. Rafiu’s courage to attack an uncertain English pass. Uzoma’s courage to stand between England and an equaliser. Akekoromowei’s courage to strike when the second goal appeared. Mamudu’s courage to arrive from the bench and finish the third. And behind all of them was a Nigerian team that refused to allow England’s periods of pressure to dictate the story. That is what makes this victory heroic. Football is often described as a game of ninety minutes, but knockout football is really a contest of emotional control. A team must know when to attack, when to absorb pressure, when to accelerate and when to remain patient. Nigeria demonstrated all four qualities. England had chances. Nigeria did not deny that reality; Nigeria simply denied England the goals those chances required. Uzoma’s penalty save became the symbol of that resistance. Rafiu’s opening goal became the symbol of Nigerian aggression. Akekoromowei’s second became the symbol of Nigeria’s ability to punish defensive uncertainty. Mamudu’s third became the signature of a team whose bench could contribute just as decisively as its starting eleven. And Moses Aduku’s Falconets now move into the quarter-finals carrying something that cannot be manufactured in a training ground: belief. The road ahead will become harder. Nigeria will face either host nation Poland or Colombia in the quarter-finals in Łódź on Sunday. ￼ But that is a story for another afternoon. For now, the images from Bielsko-Biała belong to Nigeria. The green shirts racing toward one another after the third goal. Uzoma standing tall after denying England from the penalty spot. Akekoromowei celebrating her strike. Mamudu turning a substitute’s opportunity into a World Cup moment. And an English side staring at a scoreboard that told an unmistakable story. England 0. Nigeria 3. The Falconets came to the Round of 16 knowing that one afternoon could define their tournament. They left Bielsko-Biała having defined it themselves. Nigeria did not simply advance. Nigeria announced itself. [ATIKU ABUBAKAR AND THE OBASANJO QUESTION: Can Nigeria Entrust the Presidency to a Man Whose Former President Says He Regretted Choosing Him? There is a question that deserves to sit at the centre of Nigeria’s 2027 presidential debate. It is not whether Atiku Abubakar is experienced. He is. It is not whether he has participated in Nigerian politics for decades. He has. It is not whether he understands the machinery of government. As Nigeria’s vice-president between 1999 and 2007, he occupied one of the most powerful offices in the country. The question is more fundamental: What does Atiku’s record in government tell Nigerians about the judgment, integrity, loyalty and financial accountability of the man asking them to entrust him with the presidency of the Federal Republic of Nigeria? That question cannot be answered simply by campaign slogans. It cannot be answered by saying that Atiku has never been convicted of corruption. And it cannot be answered by repeating allegations as though allegations were convictions. It requires Nigerians to examine the historical record. At the centre of that record stands the extraordinary and bitter relationship between Atiku Abubakar and former President Olusegun Obasanjo. They entered government together in 1999. They governed together for eight years. They eventually became political adversaries. And decades later, the former president is still publicly questioning the decision that brought Atiku into the presidency with him. In July 2026, Obasanjo was asked to identify the biggest mistake he made while in government. His answer was extraordinary. He said that if he had known Atiku as he came to know him later, he would not have chosen him as his running mate. When asked whether he was referring to Atiku, Obasanjo answered unequivocally: “My vice president.” ￼ This was not merely a political opponent making an accusation against another political opponent. This was a former president speaking about the man who served as his constitutional deputy for eight years. That does not make Obasanjo automatically correct. But it makes the allegation impossible to dismiss casually. WHAT DID OBASANJO ACTUALLY SAY ABOUT ATIKU? The controversy goes much deeper than Obasanjo’s 2026 statement. In his memoir, My Watch, Obasanjo devoted substantial attention to his former vice-president. He described what he said were serious concerns about Atiku’s judgment, transparency, loyalty and alleged propensity toward corruption. The memoir also recounts disputes involving Atiku’s conduct while serving as vice-president and his role in economic and privatisation matters. Among the episodes Obasanjo discussed were Atiku’s involvement with the privatisation process, alleged efforts concerning Sadiq Oil, the controversial Malabu Oil matter, and the separate American investigation involving former U.S. Congressman William Jefferson. ￼ Obasanjo’s account is an allegation and memoir testimony, not a judicial judgment. That distinction must remain intact. But there is another reason the allegations deserve examination. Obasanjo was not an outside observer. He was the president. Atiku was his vice-president. They were inside the same government. They had access to the same machinery of state. They witnessed one another’s decisions. And their relationship eventually deteriorated so badly that Atiku defected from the PDP to the Action Congress in preparation for the 2007 presidential election. The constitutional battle that followed reached the Supreme Court. THE SUPREME COURT CASE: WHAT IT DID — AND DID NOT — DECIDE This part of the history is frequently distorted in political arguments. The Supreme Court case involving Atiku in 2007 was principally a constitutional dispute concerning the status of his vice-presidential office after his political break with Obasanjo and the PDP. The legal questions included whether the president could declare the vice-presidential office vacant, whether Atiku had effectively abandoned his office by joining another political party, and the constitutional relationship between the president and vice-president. ￼ The case should therefore not be presented as though the Supreme Court convicted Atiku of corruption. It did not. This is important because credibility is built by telling Nigerians what the court actually decided rather than what political campaigns wish it had decided. But the constitutional dispute does reveal something politically relevant. The Obasanjo-Atiku relationship had deteriorated into a fundamental crisis of political trust. The president regarded his vice-president as having breached the political relationship upon which their administration had been constructed. Atiku regarded the administration’s actions against him as unconstitutional and politically motivated. The Supreme Court ultimately dealt with the constitutional questions. The political question remained. Why did the relationship between Nigeria’s president and vice-president collapse so dramatically? THE PTDF CONTROVERSY Then comes the Petroleum Technology Development Fund. This is one of the most serious historical controversies surrounding Atiku’s tenure. In 2007, a Senate investigation alleged financial improprieties involving PTDF funds. Contemporary reporting stated that a Senate committee accused Atiku of involvement in the alleged diversion of approximately $145 million belonging to PTDF to private interests and alleged that more than $4.6 million in bribes had been received. The committee also alleged that $20 million was transferred from a PTDF account without presidential approval. ￼ These are serious allegations. But they remain allegations arising from an investigation. They should not be rewritten as a criminal conviction. That distinction is essential. Atiku has consistently rejected the accusations and has argued that the confrontation with Obasanjo was intertwined with political disagreements, particularly the struggle surrounding Obasanjo’s third-term ambitions. Therefore, the appropriate question for 2027 is not: “Was Atiku convicted of stealing PTDF money?” The answer is no. The better question is: “What exactly happened to the PTDF funds, what did the investigations establish, what did Atiku’s office authorize, what documentary evidence exists, and why should Nigerians regard the matter as satisfactorily resolved?” A presidential candidate seeking the nation’s trust should welcome such scrutiny. THE $20 MILLION QUESTION The $20 million allegation deserves special attention because it illustrates the larger problem. Public money is not ordinary money. PTDF funds are not the personal resources of a vice-president. If $20 million was transferred without presidential approval, Nigerians deserve to know: Who ordered the transfer? Who authorized it? Who received it? For what purpose? Was the transaction reversed? Was the money recovered? Was anyone prosecuted? Was anyone convicted? What did the relevant investigative authorities ultimately conclude? And if Atiku maintains that the allegations were politically motivated, what evidence does he have to demonstrate that? These are not partisan questions. They are questions about the management of public resources. BUT THERE IS ANOTHER SIDE OF THE STORY — ATIKU’S $2.8 BILLION CLAIM And this is where the Atiku story becomes particularly interesting. Atiku has not presented himself merely as someone who understands government. He has also presented himself as someone with an anti-corruption record. In 2022, while campaigning for president, Atiku explained that during the Obasanjo administration he chaired a panel established to recover stolen public funds. According to his account, the panel summoned people suspected of stealing public money, confronted them with evidence, and negotiated the return of funds. Atiku said the arrangement resulted in the recovery of $2.8 billion. He presented this as a major achievement of the Obasanjo administration’s fight against corruption. ￼ That statement creates one of the most interesting accountability questions of the 2027 election. If Atiku was sufficiently trusted by President Obasanjo to chair a panel recovering billions of dollars allegedly stolen from Nigeria, why did the same administration later become so deeply divided over allegations involving Atiku himself? And if Atiku was personally responsible for helping recover $2.8 billion, where are the records? Who returned the money? How much did each person return? What institutions received the funds? How were the recovered assets valued? Were criminal prosecutions pursued? How much was recovered in cash? How much was recovered through assets? What happened to the recovered money? Were the alleged offenders ever prosecuted? And who independently audited the process? These questions matter because Atiku’s own account places him at the centre of Nigeria’s anti-corruption machinery during the Obasanjo years. The same historical period also produced allegations against him. That contradiction deserves examination. THE CENTRAL TRUST QUESTION This is where the 2027 debate should become intellectually serious. The presidency is not merely an economic office. The president controls enormous public resources. The president appoints ministers. The president influences the direction of federal agencies. The president oversees national security. The president has enormous influence over public procurement and economic policy. The president must be trusted with information that can affect the national interest. Therefore, the question of character and judgment is not a peripheral campaign issue. It is central. Obasanjo’s description of Atiku in My Watch is particularly relevant because it was written by someone who worked with him at the highest level of government. Obasanjo accused his former deputy of characteristics including a propensity toward corruption, disloyalty, poor judgment and lack of transparency. Again, these are Obasanjo’s characterizations—not findings of a court. But they raise a legitimate electoral question: If a former president who worked beside Atiku for eight years says that his choice of Atiku was his greatest mistake, why should Nigerians disregard that judgment completely? Conversely, Atiku has the right to ask Nigerians not to treat Obasanjo’s memoir as a judicial verdict. And that is exactly why the evidence should be placed before the Nigerian people. THE PROBLEM WITH BOTH EXTREMES Atiku’s defenders sometimes respond to the allegations by saying: “Show us the conviction.” That is legally correct but politically incomplete. A presidential election is not a criminal trial. Citizens are permitted to evaluate judgment, credibility, transparency and political conduct even where criminal conviction does not exist. But Atiku’s opponents make the opposite mistake when they say: “Obasanjo accused him, therefore he is a thief.” That is equally wrong. An accusation is not a conviction. A memoir is not a judgment. A Senate allegation is not necessarily a final judicial determination. Responsible voters should be capable of holding both principles simultaneously. THE QUESTION OF POLITICAL CONSISTENCY There is another issue Nigerians should examine. Atiku has occupied different political positions on major national policies over the decades. Positions can legitimately evolve. A politician is allowed to change his mind. But when a presidential candidate changes position, Nigerians should ask why. What changed? The economic evidence? The political circumstances? The country’s fiscal condition? Or the electoral calculation? That is particularly relevant when Atiku proposes policies that appear different from positions previously associated with him. The question is not whether changing one’s position is inherently wrong. It is whether the politician can explain the intellectual and economic basis for the change. EXPERIENCE IS NOT THE SAME AS TRUST Atiku’s greatest political strength is also the source of the greatest scrutiny. He has experience. But experience creates responsibility. A man who has never held national office can argue that he deserves an opportunity. A man who has spent eight years as vice-president cannot make that argument as easily. His record is already available for examination. He was inside the government. He participated in national policymaking. He witnessed the decisions of the Obasanjo administration. He subsequently became one of its fiercest critics. Now he asks Nigerians to give him the presidency. The natural democratic response is: Tell us exactly what happened. IF ATIKU WANTS THE PRESIDENCY, HE SHOULD OPEN THE FILE The most constructive challenge Atiku could receive before 2027 is not another insult from his political opponents. It is a demand for documentary transparency. Publish the relevant PTDF records. Explain the $20 million transaction. Explain the $145 million allegation. Explain the alleged $4.6 million payments. Explain the circumstances surrounding the Senate investigation. Explain the relationship with William Jefferson and the American investigation. Explain the allegations surrounding privatisation and the other matters raised by Obasanjo. Then publish the documentary evidence supporting the claim that the Obasanjo administration recovered $2.8 billion under the panel Atiku says he chaired. If the accusations are false, documentation can help destroy them. If the historical record is more complicated, Nigerians deserve to know that too. This would be far more powerful than political speeches. AND WHAT SHOULD OBASANJO BE ASKED? Accountability must run in both directions. If Obasanjo wants Nigerians to accept his judgment of Atiku, Nigerians should also ask Obasanjo difficult questions. Why did he continue working with Atiku after allegedly discovering these problems? Why did his administration not secure a criminal conviction? Why did he later reconcile politically with Atiku? Why did he support Atiku in certain political circumstances after their bitter confrontation? And what documentary evidence supports the most serious allegations in My Watch? The Nigerian people should not be required to choose between two personalities. They should be given evidence. THE PRESIDENTIAL STANDARD The presidency should require more than the absence of a criminal conviction. It should require demonstrated integrity. It should require transparency. It should require sound judgment. It should require the ability to explain one’s financial and political history. It should require the humility to acknowledge mistakes. And it should require the courage to open controversial chapters of one’s public life to independent scrutiny. That standard applies to Atiku. But it must also apply to Tinubu. It must apply to Peter Obi. It must apply to every presidential candidate. THE FINAL QUESTION FOR ATIKU Atiku Abubakar does not need Nigerians to believe that Olusegun Obasanjo is perfect. He needs to persuade Nigerians that he himself is worthy of their trust. That is a different argument. Obasanjo may have political motives. He may have personal grievances. He may have changed his views over time. All of that is possible. But none of it answers the documentary questions surrounding the controversies of the Obasanjo years. The 2027 election should therefore put one question directly before Atiku: Why should Nigerians entrust the presidency to you when the president you served beside for eight years has repeatedly raised questions about your judgment, loyalty, transparency and integrity—and what documentary evidence can you provide that conclusively answers those questions? Atiku should answer that question. Not with insults. Not with nostalgia. Not with ethnicity. Not with religion. Not with political alliances. Not with campaign slogans. With evidence. And if he can provide compelling evidence, Nigerians should examine it. If he cannot, Nigerians should ask why. That is not persecution. That is democracy. NIGERIA DESERVES A PRESIDENT WHO CAN SURVIVE THE LIGHT The Nigerian presidency is too important to be decided by mythology. Tinubu’s record must be examined. Obi’s record must be examined. Atiku’s record must be examined. The test must be identical: Show us the record. Show us the money. Show us the policy. Show us the results. Show us the evidence. Then let Nigerians decide. The 2027 election should not be a referendum on who can tell the most convincing story about himself. It should be a referendum on who can withstand the most rigorous examination of his past and still make the strongest case for Nigeria’s future. [Africa’s Currency Question: What Would America Gain—or Lose—If Africa Learned to Trade With Itself? A new economic, security and geopolitical bargain between Africa and the United States By Jide Adesina | 1stAfrika.com The most important question in the debate over African monetary integration is not whether Africa should “destroy the dollar.” It is whether Africa can become economically integrated enough to rely less on foreign currencies for its internal commerce—while becoming prosperous enough to buy far more from the United States and the rest of the world. That distinction matters. Africa does not need to overthrow the dollar. The United States does not need to fear stronger African currencies. And Africa does not need to exchange one external patron for another. What Africa needs is economic sovereignty without isolation. What the United States needs is to recognize that a more self-reliant Africa could become not a weaker client, but a larger market, a more capable security partner, a deeper investment destination, and one of America’s most important commercial relationships of the twenty-first century. The currency debate is therefore not fundamentally about banknotes. It is about production, trade, debt, infrastructure, migration, security, resources, industrialization, political accountability, and Africa’s place in the global economy. The real question is simple: Can Africa build an economy strong enough to give its people, businesses and governments more choices? Nkrumah’s unfinished argument More than six decades ago, Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, argued that political independence without economic integration would leave African countries vulnerable to outside control. In his 1963 address to the newly created Organization of African Unity, Nkrumah advocated greater continental coordination, including monetary cooperation, common economic institutions and eventually a unified African political and financial architecture. His point was not merely symbolic. A country may be politically independent and still remain economically dependent if its production, trade routes, strategic resources, financial system and development finance are controlled elsewhere. That remains true today. African economies often export commodities priced in foreign currencies, borrow in foreign currencies, import machinery and finished goods priced in foreign currencies, and settle significant trade through financial systems located outside the continent. The result is a persistent vulnerability: Africa earns hard currency from natural resources and agricultural exports, but often needs that same foreign currency to buy the technology, medicine, fuel, equipment and industrial inputs required for development. That is why the debate is not simply about replacing the dollar. It is about reducing excessive dependence on any currency or external financial system. Gaddafi, the gold dinar and historical caution No modern discussion of African monetary sovereignty can avoid Muammar Gaddafi. The former Libyan leader strongly supported African political and economic integration. He promoted the development of continental financial institutions and was associated with proposals for a more independent African monetary order. After his death in 2011, a powerful narrative emerged: that NATO intervened in Libya primarily to stop Gaddafi from launching a gold-backed African currency that would challenge the dollar and the CFA franc. The claim is politically compelling, but it should not be treated as settled history. There is evidence that Gaddafi favored greater African monetary independence and that some documents associated with the Libya conflict referred to possible plans for an African currency. But the available evidence does not establish that preventing a gold-backed currency was the decisive cause of NATO intervention or Gaddafi’s death. The more defensible conclusion is also the more important one: African monetary sovereignty would have geopolitical consequences because it would increase Africa’s bargaining power. A continent that can finance infrastructure through deeper local capital markets, process more of its own resources, settle more regional trade internally, and build credible regional reserve systems will negotiate differently with Washington, Beijing, Brussels, Moscow and the Gulf states. That is not anti-American. It is what sovereignty looks like in practice. The dollar is not Africa’s enemy The dollar remains dominant because it offers what global markets value: liquidity, convertibility, trusted legal and financial infrastructure, deep capital markets, widely accepted payment channels, and access to the world’s largest pool of investable assets. In the first quarter of 2026, the dollar accounted for 57.13% of global foreign-exchange reserves in the IMF’s COFER data.[imf] That dominance gives Washington considerable geopolitical and financial influence. It also gives African governments, companies and investors access to a highly liquid international currency. A company importing machinery from the United States can transact in dollars. An African sovereign can raise capital in global markets. An exporter can sell commodities through internationally recognized settlement systems. Banks can hold dollar assets as part of reserve and liquidity management. The problem is not the existence of the dollar. The problem is excessive dollar dependence in economies that earn largely in local currency but owe debts, import critical goods or finance infrastructure in foreign currency. When local currencies depreciate, the domestic cost of servicing dollar debt rises. Governments face fiscal stress. Banks and companies face balance-sheet pressure. Central banks lose room to maneuver. Households eventually absorb the consequences through inflation, reduced public services, or unemployment. Africa’s currency challenge is therefore less ideological than practical. It is about reducing currency mismatches and expanding economic choice. Africa’s real problem is production A common currency cannot rescue an economy that does not produce enough. If Africa created a single currency tomorrow without addressing energy shortages, infrastructure gaps, weak tax systems, uneven productivity, fragmented capital markets, governance failures, trade barriers and fiscal indiscipline, it could create a continental monetary crisis rather than continental prosperity. The lesson from Europe is instructive. The euro created a major monetary zone, but its members still differ sharply in productivity, fiscal capacity, debt levels and economic structure. Monetary integration without sufficiently strong fiscal and economic convergence can create persistent tensions. Africa is even more diverse. Nigeria’s economic structure differs from Rwanda’s. South Africa’s industrial base differs from Senegal’s. Egypt, Morocco, Kenya, Angola, Botswana and the Democratic Republic of Congo face radically different combinations of commodity exposure, demographics, fiscal capacity, infrastructure and financial development. A country facing an oil-price collapse does not necessarily need the same monetary policy as a country experiencing a manufacturing boom. That is why Africa should not begin with the slogan, “One currency now.” It should begin with a more serious objective: Build the economic architecture that could eventually sustain monetary union. Trade must come before the currency The African Continental Free Trade Area may be more important in the near term than a future African banknote. Africa’s internal trade remains low relative to other major regions. The African Development Bank reported that intra-African trade represented only about 14.4% of Africa’s total trade, reflecting fragmented production networks, weak cross-border infrastructure and persistent barriers to regional commerce.[afdb] That number reveals the deeper problem. Africa is not poor because it lacks resources. It is poor because it has not captured enough value from those resources through integrated production systems. The continent exports crude oil while importing refined fuels and petrochemicals. It exports cocoa while importing high-value chocolate and consumer products. It exports lithium, cobalt, copper and manganese but captures too little of the downstream value created in batteries, electric vehicles, electronics and advanced manufacturing. It exports cotton while importing finished garments. It exports agricultural commodities while importing processed food. The remedy is not monetary symbolism. It is industrial capability. Africa needs more regional value chains, reliable energy, ports, railways, roads, digital payment systems, manufacturing clusters, agricultural processing, pharmaceutical production, technical skills, research institutions and long-term industrial finance. A currency becomes credible because the economy behind it is credible. No central bank can permanently compensate for a continent that imports too much, produces too little and lacks the institutional capacity to manage its finances. Why America should welcome a stronger Africa A more integrated African monetary system would reduce some demand for the dollar in intra-African trade. It could diminish transaction revenues for some foreign banks and reduce a measure of Washington’s financial leverage. Those losses are real. But they are likely to be smaller than the gains from a richer and more productive African market. In 2025, U.S. goods trade with Sub-Saharan Africa totaled approximately $56.4 billion. U.S. services trade with the region totaled about $23.1 billion.[ustr] Those are significant figures, but they remain modest compared with the long-term opportunity represented by Africa’s demographics, urbanization, rising consumer markets, technology adoption and infrastructure needs. Africa’s population surpassed 1.5 billion in 2024 and is projected to approach 2.5 billion by 2050. The economic significance is not merely population growth. It is the expansion of a workforce, consumer base and entrepreneurial class that could reshape global demand.[uneca] A wealthier Africa would buy more software, medical technology, cloud services, agricultural technology, industrial equipment, aviation products, financial services, cybersecurity tools, educational services and entertainment. America’s strategic mistake would be to confuse African independence with anti-Americanism. A more prosperous Africa would not necessarily buy less from the United States. It could buy substantially more. What the United States could do The United States should not seek to obstruct African monetary integration. It should help make African economic integration more credible, transparent and commercially viable. An effective Africa policy would focus less on dependency and more on capacity. • Support interoperable African payment systems and secure digital financial infrastructure. • Expand local-currency financing for viable infrastructure and private-sector investment. • Help deepen African capital markets and strengthen financial-sector regulation. • Invest in industrial corridors, logistics networks and reliable electricity. • Build partnerships around African critical-mineral processing, rather than simply extraction. • Support technical training, scientific research and manufacturing capability. • Encourage U.S. firms to establish production, research and service operations across African markets. • Build investment frameworks that are transparent, rules-based and resistant to corruption. • Treat African governments as economic partners rather than aid recipients. This is not charity. It is strategic self-interest. A United States that helps African economies become more capable, more integrated and more productive will gain access to stronger markets, more resilient supply chains and more stable partners. The limits of a currency union Africa would gain from better regional settlement systems, local-currency trade, stronger cross-border payment infrastructure and deeper domestic capital markets. But a continental currency would also involve major risks. Countries would lose some ability to use exchange rates and national monetary policy to respond to local shocks. A financially reckless government could create pressure across the union. Inflation in a major economy could become a regional problem. Stronger economies could face political resistance if they are seen as permanently financing weaker ones. A credible African monetary union would therefore require far more than an African Central Bank. It would require: • Clear fiscal rules and credible enforcement. • Independent central-bank governance. • Transparent reserve management and audited accounts. • Strong banking supervision. • Reliable cross-border payment and settlement systems. • Deposit protection and crisis-resolution mechanisms. • Economic-convergence targets. • Rules limiting political financing by central banks. • Institutions capable of managing regional economic shocks. • Public confidence that monetary policy serves citizens rather than political elites. Without these safeguards, a continental currency could become a grand political symbol with weak economic foundations. Jobs, migration and security The strongest argument for African economic integration is not currency. It is employment. Sub-Saharan Africa’s working-age population is expected to expand by more than 600 million over the next quarter-century. Yet wage-paying work remains scarce: the World Bank reports that wage-paying employment accounts for only about 24% of employment in the region.[worldbank +1] This is the real migration equation. People do not leave their homes because they dislike their countries. They leave because they believe their chances of building a dignified life are better elsewhere. A young person who sees no path to stable work, business formation, education, safety or social mobility may choose dangerous migration because staying appears more dangerous economically. A currency alone will not change that. But regional trade, industrial employment, technology ecosystems, energy investment, agricultural processing and access to finance can. If a Nigerian can build a company in Lagos, if a Kenyan can work in an expanding technology economy, if a Ghanaian can participate in a regional food-processing industry, if Congolese minerals can support battery manufacturing in Africa, and if young Africans can find dignified work closer to home, the incentive for irregular migration can decline. Not disappear—but decline. The same principle applies to security. Poverty does not automatically produce terrorism. But unemployment, exclusion, weak institutions, corruption, state absence and economic frustration can create environments in which criminal networks and extremist groups recruit more easily. Military operations may disrupt armed groups. They cannot substitute for jobs, functioning schools, legitimate institutions and economic hope. You can destroy a terrorist camp. You cannot bomb unemployment. The new Atlantic bargain Africa’s future should not be defined by opposition to America. Nor should it be defined by continued dependence on America, China, Europe, Russia or the Gulf states. Africa needs strategic autonomy: the ability to trade, borrow, invest, manufacture and negotiate from a position of greater strength. That means currency plurality, not merely currency replacement. The dollar should remain available. So should the euro, the yuan and other international currencies. But African currencies should become more stable, more usable and more widely accepted in African trade. Regional settlement systems should expand. Local capital markets should deepen. An eventual continental monetary unit should be treated as a long-term destination, not an immediate political shortcut. The United States, meanwhile, should understand that its greatest strength has never been that others remain weak. America became powerful because it built institutions, markets, technology, infrastructure, innovation and productive capacity that the world wanted to use. Africa’s task is not to imitate America’s history. It is to build its own economic capacity. America’s task is not to prevent that rise. It is to compete fairly within it and participate profitably in it. The final question Would the United States lose something if Africa settled more of its own trade in African currencies? Yes. The dollar could lose a portion of its role in African commerce. U.S. financial institutions could lose some transaction revenue. Washington’s sanctions leverage could be less decisive in a more diversified payment environment. But America could gain something larger: a continent of more prosperous consumers, producers, investors and strategic partners. Africa, meanwhile, would gain more than a currency. It would gain choices. Choice about where to work. Choice about where to invest. Choice about where to build businesses. Choice about whether migration is an opportunity or a necessity. Choice about which partners to engage. Choice about whether its resources leave as raw materials or return as expensive finished goods. That is the real meaning of economic sovereignty. Africa should not begin with a continental currency. It should begin with trade. Then production. Then infrastructure. Then interoperable payments. Then deeper capital markets. Then regulatory convergence. Then fiscal discipline. Then credible institutions. Only after those foundations are durable should Africa seriously consider a common currency. The African Union’s long-term vision already includes continental financial institutions and eventual monetary integration. The challenge is not imagination. It is execution. Africa does not need to escape America. Africa needs to stop needing permission. And America does not need to fear African independence. It needs to recognize that a productive, integrated and prosperous Africa could become one of the United States’ most consequential partners in the global economy. The future should not belong to a world in which Africa is permanently dependent on the dollar. Nor should it belong to a world in which America fears a financially capable Africa. Title: Eighty Years On: The United Nations, Its Origins, Trials, and the Road Ahead

Jide Adesina | 1stafrika.com

Eighty years ago, in the ashes of the Second World War, the international community attempted something humanity had never successfully achieved before: a permanent global mechanism to prevent another descent into total war. The United Nations was born in 1945 not merely as an institution, but as a moral response to catastrophe. Its formation reflected a shared realization that unchecked nationalism, power politics, and indifference to human suffering had brought the world to the brink of annihilation—and that survival now depended on cooperation.

The UN emerged from the failure of the League of Nations, whose inability to enforce collective security had allowed fascism and militarism to flourish in the 1930s. This time, the architects of the post-war order—led by the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, China, and France—sought to build a system with both legitimacy and authority. The UN Charter, signed in San Francisco in June 1945, committed member states to uphold international peace and security, promote human rights, encourage social and economic development, and respect the sovereign equality of nations, large and small.

At its core, the UN was designed to manage power without war. The Security Council, with its five permanent members, reflected the geopolitical realities of 1945, granting veto power to the victors of World War II in exchange for their continued participation. The General Assembly offered a universal forum where all states could speak, while specialized agencies—from the World Health Organization to UNESCO—addressed humanity’s shared challenges beyond the battlefield.

Over eight decades, the United Nations has left an indelible mark on global affairs. It has helped prevent another world war, facilitated decolonization across Africa and Asia, coordinated humanitarian relief during famines and conflicts, advanced international law, and articulated universal norms through instruments like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. UN peacekeeping missions, though imperfect, have helped stabilize post-conflict societies and reduce the likelihood of renewed violence in dozens of regions.

Yet the UN’s history is equally defined by its limitations. The Cold War paralyzed the Security Council for decades, turning the organization into a stage for ideological confrontation rather than collective action. In the post–Cold War era, new challenges emerged: intra-state conflicts, terrorism, climate change, pandemics, cyber warfare, and mass displacement—threats the UN was never originally designed to confront. The veto power has repeatedly blocked action in crises such as Syria, Palestine, Ukraine, and Sudan, exposing a credibility gap between the UN’s principles and its political realities.

Critics argue that the organization is overly bureaucratic, slow to act, and structurally biased in favor of powerful states. The composition of the Security Council no longer reflects today’s world, where Africa, Latin America, and much of Asia remain underrepresented in global decision-making. Funding constraints, selective enforcement of international law, and the erosion of multilateralism have further weakened the UN’s authority.

Despite these challenges, the United Nations remains indispensable. No other institution provides a global platform where nearly every country can engage, negotiate, and coordinate responses to shared crises. During the COVID-19 pandemic, climate negotiations, refugee emergencies, and development financing debates, the UN continues to serve as the backbone of international cooperation—often quietly, imperfectly, but persistently.

The hope for the UN’s future lies in reform and renewal, not abandonment. Meaningful Security Council reform, greater inclusion of the Global South, stronger accountability mechanisms, and increased investment in prevention rather than reaction are essential if the organization is to remain relevant. Equally important is the political will of member states to treat the UN not as a convenient scapegoat, but as a collective responsibility.

Eighty years after its founding, the United Nations stands at a crossroads. The world is again fragmented, trust between major powers is eroding, and global crises are multiplying. Yet the original truth that gave birth to the UN remains unchanged: global problems cannot be solved by nations acting alone. The UN is neither a world government nor a cure-all, but it is humanity’s best attempt to replace chaos with dialogue and conflict with cooperation.

Its future will ultimately reflect the choices of its members. If nations choose rivalry over responsibility, the UN will weaken. If they choose reform, solidarity, and respect for shared rules, the United Nations can continue to serve as a fragile but vital guardian of peace in an increasingly uncertain world. | 1st Afrika Times International

[Female Genital Mutilation in Africa: The Cut That Tradition Must Not Defend By Jide Adesina | 1stAfrika.com There are wounds that close with time. Others remain long after the skin has healed. Female genital mutilation belongs to the second category. Across parts of Africa, generations of girls and women carry the lasting physical and psychological consequences of a practice sustained by social expectation, cultural inheritance, and communal pressure. Some were cut as infants. Others were children barely old enough to understand what was happening. Many were told the procedure was essential for womanhood, dignity, marriage prospects, or acceptance. Beneath those explanations lies a more fundamental question: when does tradition cease to be cultural inheritance and become an injury imposed on the powerless? Female genital mutilation (FGM) involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, or other injury to the female genital organs, for non-medical reasons. The World Health Organization classifies four types, with consequences that include severe pain, bleeding, infection, urinary and menstrual difficulties, sexual complications, and serious risks in childbirth. In some cases, the outcome is fatal. The scale is vast. UNICEF estimates that more than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone FGM in countries with nationally representative data. More than 144 million of them live in Africa—the region bearing the largest share of the global burden. Yet Africa must not be reduced to a statistic. Africa is not one culture, one people, or one tradition. It is a continent of more than a billion people, thousands of ethnic communities, languages, histories, and belief systems. FGM is concentrated in particular societies. Its prevalence varies sharply from country to country and community to community. Describing it simply as an “African tradition” obscures the many communities working to end it and unfairly burdens an entire continent with a single practice. The real story is more complicated—and far more human. The Child Behind the Statistic Imagine a child taken into a room by adults she trusts. She may be told little. She may be frightened. She may not understand why she is there. The adults surrounding her may regard the procedure as normal because it was performed on their mothers, sisters, and grandmothers. For the child there is no historical context—only the immediate experience of pain, fear, confusion, and, in many cases, blood. FGM is most commonly performed in childhood, often before the age of 15. The younger the child, the sharper the question of consent. A child cannot meaningfully weigh lifelong consequences she does not understand and may not even know she has the right to refuse. This is why the discussion must move beyond culture into the territory of children’s rights, bodily autonomy, and protection from harm. The girl is not an abstract vessel for tradition. She is a human being. Why the Practice Continues It is tempting to portray families who permit FGM as cruel or ignorant. That portrayal may satisfy outsiders seeking simplicity, but it fails to capture the social machinery that keeps the practice alive. In many communities, families respond to powerful expectations. Parents may fear that an uncircumcised daughter will be rejected. A mother may worry about her daughter’s marriage prospects. A family may believe refusal brings shame. An older woman may insist on the practice because she underwent it herself and believes she is preserving community values. This creates one of the most disturbing paradoxes of FGM: people who were subjected to it can become its guardians. The cycle is often sustained less by individual cruelty than by conformity. When everyone believes everyone else expects the practice to continue, breaking away becomes extraordinarily difficult. Eliminating FGM therefore cannot rest solely on telling individual parents to behave differently. Entire communities must be given the social permission—and the practical support—to change together. Tradition Is Not Beyond Question Africa has always possessed traditions. Yet African civilization has never been static. Cultures evolve. Institutions change. Practices disappear. New values emerge. Old customs are reinterpreted. The argument that something must continue simply because it is old is inadequate. Age does not confer moral legitimacy. A tradition can carry identity and meaning while still containing practices that society eventually decides to abandon. The question is not whether Africans should preserve their culture. They should. The question is whether cultural preservation requires the permanent injury of children. It does not. Africa does not have to choose between identity and human dignity. A society can protect its language, music, ceremonies, family structures, spirituality, history, and communal values while rejecting practices that cause preventable harm. The Body Remembers The consequences of FGM extend far beyond the day it occurs. Immediate and long-term complications can include severe bleeding, infections, urinary problems, menstrual difficulties, chronic pain, psychological trauma, sexual complications, and life-threatening risks during childbirth. For some women the experience becomes a lifelong medical reality. For others it is a psychological wound. For many it is both. There is also a broader economic cost. The World Health Organization has estimated that treating health complications associated with FGM costs health systems approximately $1.4 billion every year. Behind that figure stand hospitals, clinicians, medicines, emergency procedures, and women requiring care for conditions that should never have existed. The cost is not merely financial. It is human. The Dangerous Illusion of “Medicalized” FGM One misconception that has gained ground is that FGM becomes acceptable or safe when performed by a healthcare professional. It does not. A medical setting cannot create medical necessity where none exists. The World Health Organization opposes the medicalization of FGM and urges health professionals not to perform it. A sterile instrument does not transform a harmful non-medical procedure into a beneficial one. The issue is not the training of the person holding the instrument. The issue is why the procedure is being performed at all. Religion Is Not the Whole Explanation FGM is sometimes presented as if it belonged exclusively to one religion. That explanation is historically and socially inadequate. The practice exists among communities of different religious identities and predates many contemporary religious institutions. Reducing it to religion obscures its deeper roots in social norms, gender expectations, and community practices. Religious leaders nevertheless have an important role. Where communities believe FGM is religiously required, respected authorities can help dismantle that misconception. The goal is not to attack faith. It is to prevent faith from being misused as justification for harming children. African Women Leading the Resistance Perhaps the most important part of this story is the resistance already underway. African women are not passive victims waiting for outsiders to rescue them. Survivors are speaking. Activists are organizing. Health professionals are treating survivors. Teachers are educating children. Community leaders are challenging inherited expectations. Young people are questioning practices their parents once accepted without question. Across the continent, women and girls themselves are among the strongest voices for ending FGM. Sustainable change cannot be imposed permanently from outside. Communities must eventually own the decision to abandon the practice. When a grandmother says, “It ends with me,” the cycle begins to break. When a father says, “My daughter will not be cut,” the social equation shifts. When a community declares that its girls can remain uncut and still be respected, marriageable, and fully accepted members of society, the foundation supporting FGM begins to collapse. Nigeria’s Complicated Reality Nigeria illustrates why statistics must be handled with care. The country has one of Africa’s largest populations, and FGM does not occur uniformly. UNICEF data place prevalence among women and girls aged 15 to 49 at approximately 15 percent nationally, with substantial differences between states, regions, and communities. A national percentage should never conceal individual suffering. Even a comparatively lower national rate can represent millions of affected women and girls in a country of Nigeria’s size. Nigeria has enacted legal and policy measures, including provisions under the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act. Legislation alone, however, cannot dismantle a social practice. A law can prohibit. A community must transform. That transformation requires education, enforcement, healthcare, protection for vulnerable girls, and sustained engagement with families, traditional institutions, religious authorities, and young people. Men Cannot Remain Spectators The conversation about FGM has historically centered on women and girls—understandably, because they are the people most directly affected. Yet men hold enormous influence over the social conditions that allow the practice to survive. Fathers can refuse to permit it. Husbands can reject the notion that an uncut woman is unsuitable for marriage. Community leaders can speak against it. Young men can challenge expectations passed down through generations. Protecting girls is a responsibility shared by the entire society. A Continent Changing Its Mind There is evidence that attitudes can shift. UNICEF reports significant declines in FGM prevalence among younger generations in several countries. That progress matters because it demonstrates that practices once considered immovable can move. The challenge remains immense. Population growth means that even when prevalence declines, the absolute number of girls at risk can remain extremely high. Africa can be making progress while millions of girls remain vulnerable. Both realities can exist at once. The response cannot be complacency. Nor should it be despair. It must be acceleration. Beyond Condemnation Ending FGM requires more than condemnation. It requires understanding the social system that surrounds the practice. It requires protecting girls who refuse. It requires services for survivors. It requires trained healthcare workers, accurate data, education, enforced laws, and economic alternatives where livelihoods have become tied to the practice. Above all, it requires genuine community dialogue. Most importantly, it requires listening to survivors. Too often, women who endured FGM become objects of discussion rather than participants in the conversation. Their stories should not be harvested merely for emotional effect. They should help shape policy, influence healthcare, inform education, and determine what support systems look like. The survivor must not disappear once her story has generated public attention. The Girl Who Has Not Yet Been Cut Somewhere in Africa tonight, a girl is sleeping. She may be six. She may be ten. She may be fourteen. She does not know the statistics or the language of international conventions. She simply knows that she wants to grow up, go to school, laugh with her friends, and become whatever she imagines becoming. Her future should not depend on whether adults decide that pain is necessary for her acceptance. Somewhere else, another woman lives with the consequences of what happened to her as a child. She does not need pity. She needs dignity, healthcare when she requires it, psychological support when she needs it, and a society willing to listen when she speaks. She deserves the right to define herself beyond what was done to her body. A survivor is not her wound. A girl is not a ritual. A woman is not a tradition. She is a person. Africa’s Choice The future of Africa will be shaped by its economies, its technology, its governments, its young population, and its growing cities. It will also be measured by how it treats its children. The continent does not need to reject its heritage to reject FGM. It does not need to surrender its identity to protect its daughters. It needs only to recognize that cultures are strongest when they have the courage to examine themselves. There is nothing uniquely African about refusing to change—and nothing uniquely African about change itself. African societies have reinvented themselves countless times throughout history. They can do so again. The end of FGM will not come because outsiders declare Africa backward. It will come when African families, women, men, elders, young people, governments, traditional authorities, religious leaders, and communities decide that the dignity of the girl is more important than the pressure to conform. The transformation begins when a mother chooses differently. When a father speaks. When an elder changes her mind. When a community breaks the silence. When a survivor is believed. When a girl is allowed to say no. And when society finally understands that protecting tradition can never mean sacrificing the child who is expected to inherit it. Female genital mutilation is not merely about a cut. It is about who has the power to decide what happens to a child’s body. That is why the conversation must continue—not with hatred, not with contempt for African cultures, and not with silence, but with evidence, courage, compassion, and the determination to ensure that the next generation of African girls inherits a continent where womanhood does not have to begin with pain. [When the Falconets Took England Apart: Nigeria’s 3–0 Masterclass in Bielsko-Biała By Jide Adesina | 1stAfrika.com There are football victories that arrive quietly, recorded in the statistics and quickly forgotten. Then there are victories that announce themselves with the force of a national statement. Nigeria’s 3–0 demolition of England in the Round of 16 of the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland belonged firmly to the second category. On Thursday afternoon in Bielsko-Biała, the Falconets did not merely survive a knockout contest. They walked into the Stadion Miejski with the authority of a team that had decided that England would not be allowed to write the next chapter of Nigeria’s World Cup story. And by the time the final whistle came, Nigeria had written it themselves. The scoreboard was brutally simple: England 0, Nigeria 3. Tosin Rafiu had struck early. Seimeyeha Janet Akekoromowei had doubled the advantage almost immediately after halftime. Mary Mamudu had delivered the final blow in the 73rd minute. Between those goals stood another story altogether: a goalkeeper who refused to surrender, a defence that absorbed pressure, a midfield that repeatedly disrupted England’s rhythm, and an attack that punished every opening. ￼ The stadium had barely settled into the afternoon when Nigeria delivered its first warning. Eight minutes were on the clock when Rafiu turned an English mistake into Nigerian opportunity. She intercepted a loose pass high up the pitch, accelerated into the penalty area and, from an increasingly difficult angle, found the finish that sent the ball beyond Katie Cox. It was not simply an early goal. It changed the psychological landscape of the match. England had entered the knockout stage knowing that one mistake could be fatal. Nigeria immediately demonstrated why. The Falconets were not going to wait patiently for England to establish control. They were going to attack the spaces, challenge the English defenders and force the Young Lionesses to play under pressure. England responded. That response is important because the 3–0 scoreline should not obscure what happened in the opening half. England created opportunities and, for stretches, threatened seriously. Princess Ademiluyi found space, Lily Dent pushed forward and Rachel Maltby became increasingly involved. Nigeria’s defence was being tested, and this was where Christiana Uzoma began to write her own chapter of the afternoon. The Nigerian goalkeeper was magnificent. She was not simply a spectator behind a defence protecting a one-goal advantage. She was repeatedly required to rescue it. One of her most important interventions came when Ademiluyi found herself with a clear opportunity. Uzoma stood her ground and made the save. Another English attack followed, and again Uzoma was there. Then came the moment that could have transformed the entire contest. England won a penalty after a lengthy VAR review following a foul on Ademiluyi. Rachel Maltby stood over the ball with Nigeria’s early advantage suddenly under direct threat. The stadium waited. Maltby struck. Uzoma reacted. The Nigerian goalkeeper got enough on the penalty to push it onto the crossbar, preserving Nigeria’s 1–0 lead. ￼ That save was more than a goalkeeping statistic. It was the emotional hinge of the match. Had England equalised before halftime, the entire complexion of the contest could have changed. Instead, Nigeria walked into the dressing room still ahead. The Falconets had survived England’s best first-half examination. But survival was never going to be enough. When Nigeria emerged for the second half, they returned with the urgency of a team determined to settle the argument. Two minutes after the restart, the English defence failed to properly clear a corner. The ball remained alive inside the danger area and Akekoromowei reacted with devastating precision. She struck. The ball found the net. Nigeria 2, England 0. Suddenly England were no longer chasing an equaliser. They were chasing a way back into a match that Nigeria was beginning to own. ￼ The second goal revealed another quality in this Nigerian side: ruthlessness. The Falconets did not need to dominate possession every second. They understood where the match could be won. They pressed when England were vulnerable, defended when England attacked and moved forward with purpose when the opportunity appeared. England tried to respond with substitutions and increased attacking pressure. But Nigeria’s structure remained remarkably difficult to break. And then came the third. The clock moved into the 73rd minute when Akekoromowei again became central to the attack. She won the ball near the byline after England struggled to deal with the situation and squared it into the danger area. Mary Mamudu had entered the match as a substitute in the 61st minute. Twelve minutes later, she delivered the decisive moment. Mamudu met the opportunity and finished into an unguarded net. Nigeria 3, England 0. The English resistance had been broken. The Falconets now had something far more valuable than a lead. They had control of the match. England continued to push, but Nigeria’s defenders had learned the rhythm of the opposition. Attempts were blocked. Attacks were disrupted. England were repeatedly caught offside, and when they did manage to find a path toward goal, Uzoma and the Nigerian defence stood between them and redemption. ￼ The closing stages became a demonstration of Nigerian composure. Moses Aduku used his bench intelligently, bringing on fresh legs to maintain the intensity and protect the advantage. Victory Lucky, Winner Onajite David and Folajomi Olabiyi entered as Nigeria managed the final stages. There was no panic. No desperate retreat. No collapse under pressure. Nigeria played like a team that understood exactly what the scoreboard meant and exactly what was required to get to the quarter-finals. When the referee finally ended the contest, the Nigerian players could celebrate what they had accomplished. England had been eliminated. Nigeria had advanced. And the manner of the victory made it particularly significant. The Falconets had not reached the quarter-finals through a narrow escape or a penalty shootout. They had defeated England by three clear goals while keeping a clean sheet. The result also represented the biggest World Cup victory in a meeting between Nigeria and England across their men’s and women’s senior and U-20 teams, according to reporting from ACLSports. ￼ For Nigeria, the victory also continued a remarkable scoring run. After four matches, the Falconets had scored 13 goals in the tournament. ￼ But numbers alone cannot explain what happened in Bielsko-Biała. This was a performance built around moments of courage. Rafiu’s courage to attack an uncertain English pass. Uzoma’s courage to stand between England and an equaliser. Akekoromowei’s courage to strike when the second goal appeared. Mamudu’s courage to arrive from the bench and finish the third. And behind all of them was a Nigerian team that refused to allow England’s periods of pressure to dictate the story. That is what makes this victory heroic. Football is often described as a game of ninety minutes, but knockout football is really a contest of emotional control. A team must know when to attack, when to absorb pressure, when to accelerate and when to remain patient. Nigeria demonstrated all four qualities. England had chances. Nigeria did not deny that reality; Nigeria simply denied England the goals those chances required. Uzoma’s penalty save became the symbol of that resistance. Rafiu’s opening goal became the symbol of Nigerian aggression. Akekoromowei’s second became the symbol of Nigeria’s ability to punish defensive uncertainty. Mamudu’s third became the signature of a team whose bench could contribute just as decisively as its starting eleven. And Moses Aduku’s Falconets now move into the quarter-finals carrying something that cannot be manufactured in a training ground: belief. The road ahead will become harder. Nigeria will face either host nation Poland or Colombia in the quarter-finals in Łódź on Sunday. ￼ But that is a story for another afternoon. For now, the images from Bielsko-Biała belong to Nigeria. The green shirts racing toward one another after the third goal. Uzoma standing tall after denying England from the penalty spot. Akekoromowei celebrating her strike. Mamudu turning a substitute’s opportunity into a World Cup moment. And an English side staring at a scoreboard that told an unmistakable story. England 0. Nigeria 3. The Falconets came to the Round of 16 knowing that one afternoon could define their tournament. They left Bielsko-Biała having defined it themselves. Nigeria did not simply advance. Nigeria announced itself.
