[ATIKU ABUBAKAR AND THE OBASANJO QUESTION: Can Nigeria Entrust the Presidency to a Man Whose Former President Says He Regretted Choosing Him? There is a question that deserves to sit at the centre of Nigeria’s 2027 presidential debate. It is not whether Atiku Abubakar is experienced. He is. It is not whether he has participated in Nigerian politics for decades. He has. It is not whether he understands the machinery of government. As Nigeria’s vice-president between 1999 and 2007, he occupied one of the most powerful offices in the country. The question is more fundamental: What does Atiku’s record in government tell Nigerians about the judgment, integrity, loyalty and financial accountability of the man asking them to entrust him with the presidency of the Federal Republic of Nigeria? That question cannot be answered simply by campaign slogans. It cannot be answered by saying that Atiku has never been convicted of corruption. And it cannot be answered by repeating allegations as though allegations were convictions. It requires Nigerians to examine the historical record. At the centre of that record stands the extraordinary and bitter relationship between Atiku Abubakar and former President Olusegun Obasanjo. They entered government together in 1999. They governed together for eight years. They eventually became political adversaries. And decades later, the former president is still publicly questioning the decision that brought Atiku into the presidency with him. In July 2026, Obasanjo was asked to identify the biggest mistake he made while in government. His answer was extraordinary. He said that if he had known Atiku as he came to know him later, he would not have chosen him as his running mate. When asked whether he was referring to Atiku, Obasanjo answered unequivocally: “My vice president.” ￼ This was not merely a political opponent making an accusation against another political opponent. This was a former president speaking about the man who served as his constitutional deputy for eight years. That does not make Obasanjo automatically correct. But it makes the allegation impossible to dismiss casually. WHAT DID OBASANJO ACTUALLY SAY ABOUT ATIKU? The controversy goes much deeper than Obasanjo’s 2026 statement. In his memoir, My Watch, Obasanjo devoted substantial attention to his former vice-president. He described what he said were serious concerns about Atiku’s judgment, transparency, loyalty and alleged propensity toward corruption. The memoir also recounts disputes involving Atiku’s conduct while serving as vice-president and his role in economic and privatisation matters. Among the episodes Obasanjo discussed were Atiku’s involvement with the privatisation process, alleged efforts concerning Sadiq Oil, the controversial Malabu Oil matter, and the separate American investigation involving former U.S. Congressman William Jefferson. ￼ Obasanjo’s account is an allegation and memoir testimony, not a judicial judgment. That distinction must remain intact. But there is another reason the allegations deserve examination. Obasanjo was not an outside observer. He was the president. Atiku was his vice-president. They were inside the same government. They had access to the same machinery of state. They witnessed one another’s decisions. And their relationship eventually deteriorated so badly that Atiku defected from the PDP to the Action Congress in preparation for the 2007 presidential election. The constitutional battle that followed reached the Supreme Court. THE SUPREME COURT CASE: WHAT IT DID — AND DID NOT — DECIDE This part of the history is frequently distorted in political arguments. The Supreme Court case involving Atiku in 2007 was principally a constitutional dispute concerning the status of his vice-presidential office after his political break with Obasanjo and the PDP. The legal questions included whether the president could declare the vice-presidential office vacant, whether Atiku had effectively abandoned his office by joining another political party, and the constitutional relationship between the president and vice-president. ￼ The case should therefore not be presented as though the Supreme Court convicted Atiku of corruption. It did not. This is important because credibility is built by telling Nigerians what the court actually decided rather than what political campaigns wish it had decided. But the constitutional dispute does reveal something politically relevant. The Obasanjo-Atiku relationship had deteriorated into a fundamental crisis of political trust. The president regarded his vice-president as having breached the political relationship upon which their administration had been constructed. Atiku regarded the administration’s actions against him as unconstitutional and politically motivated. The Supreme Court ultimately dealt with the constitutional questions. The political question remained. Why did the relationship between Nigeria’s president and vice-president collapse so dramatically? THE PTDF CONTROVERSY Then comes the Petroleum Technology Development Fund. This is one of the most serious historical controversies surrounding Atiku’s tenure. In 2007, a Senate investigation alleged financial improprieties involving PTDF funds. Contemporary reporting stated that a Senate committee accused Atiku of involvement in the alleged diversion of approximately $145 million belonging to PTDF to private interests and alleged that more than $4.6 million in bribes had been received. The committee also alleged that $20 million was transferred from a PTDF account without presidential approval. ￼ These are serious allegations. But they remain allegations arising from an investigation. They should not be rewritten as a criminal conviction. That distinction is essential. Atiku has consistently rejected the accusations and has argued that the confrontation with Obasanjo was intertwined with political disagreements, particularly the struggle surrounding Obasanjo’s third-term ambitions. Therefore, the appropriate question for 2027 is not: “Was Atiku convicted of stealing PTDF money?” The answer is no. The better question is: “What exactly happened to the PTDF funds, what did the investigations establish, what did Atiku’s office authorize, what documentary evidence exists, and why should Nigerians regard the matter as satisfactorily resolved?” A presidential candidate seeking the nation’s trust should welcome such scrutiny. THE $20 MILLION QUESTION The $20 million allegation deserves special attention because it illustrates the larger problem. Public money is not ordinary money. PTDF funds are not the personal resources of a vice-president. If $20 million was transferred without presidential approval, Nigerians deserve to know: Who ordered the transfer? Who authorized it? Who received it? For what purpose? Was the transaction reversed? Was the money recovered? Was anyone prosecuted? Was anyone convicted? What did the relevant investigative authorities ultimately conclude? And if Atiku maintains that the allegations were politically motivated, what evidence does he have to demonstrate that? These are not partisan questions. They are questions about the management of public resources. BUT THERE IS ANOTHER SIDE OF THE STORY — ATIKU’S $2.8 BILLION CLAIM And this is where the Atiku story becomes particularly interesting. Atiku has not presented himself merely as someone who understands government. He has also presented himself as someone with an anti-corruption record. In 2022, while campaigning for president, Atiku explained that during the Obasanjo administration he chaired a panel established to recover stolen public funds. According to his account, the panel summoned people suspected of stealing public money, confronted them with evidence, and negotiated the return of funds. Atiku said the arrangement resulted in the recovery of $2.8 billion. He presented this as a major achievement of the Obasanjo administration’s fight against corruption. ￼ That statement creates one of the most interesting accountability questions of the 2027 election. If Atiku was sufficiently trusted by President Obasanjo to chair a panel recovering billions of dollars allegedly stolen from Nigeria, why did the same administration later become so deeply divided over allegations involving Atiku himself? And if Atiku was personally responsible for helping recover $2.8 billion, where are the records? Who returned the money? How much did each person return? What institutions received the funds? How were the recovered assets valued? Were criminal prosecutions pursued? How much was recovered in cash? How much was recovered through assets? What happened to the recovered money? Were the alleged offenders ever prosecuted? And who independently audited the process? These questions matter because Atiku’s own account places him at the centre of Nigeria’s anti-corruption machinery during the Obasanjo years. The same historical period also produced allegations against him. That contradiction deserves examination. THE CENTRAL TRUST QUESTION This is where the 2027 debate should become intellectually serious. The presidency is not merely an economic office. The president controls enormous public resources. The president appoints ministers. The president influences the direction of federal agencies. The president oversees national security. The president has enormous influence over public procurement and economic policy. The president must be trusted with information that can affect the national interest. Therefore, the question of character and judgment is not a peripheral campaign issue. It is central. Obasanjo’s description of Atiku in My Watch is particularly relevant because it was written by someone who worked with him at the highest level of government. Obasanjo accused his former deputy of characteristics including a propensity toward corruption, disloyalty, poor judgment and lack of transparency. Again, these are Obasanjo’s characterizations—not findings of a court. But they raise a legitimate electoral question: If a former president who worked beside Atiku for eight years says that his choice of Atiku was his greatest mistake, why should Nigerians disregard that judgment completely? Conversely, Atiku has the right to ask Nigerians not to treat Obasanjo’s memoir as a judicial verdict. And that is exactly why the evidence should be placed before the Nigerian people. THE PROBLEM WITH BOTH EXTREMES Atiku’s defenders sometimes respond to the allegations by saying: “Show us the conviction.” That is legally correct but politically incomplete. A presidential election is not a criminal trial. Citizens are permitted to evaluate judgment, credibility, transparency and political conduct even where criminal conviction does not exist. But Atiku’s opponents make the opposite mistake when they say: “Obasanjo accused him, therefore he is a thief.” That is equally wrong. An accusation is not a conviction. A memoir is not a judgment. A Senate allegation is not necessarily a final judicial determination. Responsible voters should be capable of holding both principles simultaneously. THE QUESTION OF POLITICAL CONSISTENCY There is another issue Nigerians should examine. Atiku has occupied different political positions on major national policies over the decades. Positions can legitimately evolve. A politician is allowed to change his mind. But when a presidential candidate changes position, Nigerians should ask why. What changed? The economic evidence? The political circumstances? The country’s fiscal condition? Or the electoral calculation? That is particularly relevant when Atiku proposes policies that appear different from positions previously associated with him. The question is not whether changing one’s position is inherently wrong. It is whether the politician can explain the intellectual and economic basis for the change. EXPERIENCE IS NOT THE SAME AS TRUST Atiku’s greatest political strength is also the source of the greatest scrutiny. He has experience. But experience creates responsibility. A man who has never held national office can argue that he deserves an opportunity. A man who has spent eight years as vice-president cannot make that argument as easily. His record is already available for examination. He was inside the government. He participated in national policymaking. He witnessed the decisions of the Obasanjo administration. He subsequently became one of its fiercest critics. Now he asks Nigerians to give him the presidency. The natural democratic response is: Tell us exactly what happened. IF ATIKU WANTS THE PRESIDENCY, HE SHOULD OPEN THE FILE The most constructive challenge Atiku could receive before 2027 is not another insult from his political opponents. It is a demand for documentary transparency. Publish the relevant PTDF records. Explain the $20 million transaction. Explain the $145 million allegation. Explain the alleged $4.6 million payments. Explain the circumstances surrounding the Senate investigation. Explain the relationship with William Jefferson and the American investigation. Explain the allegations surrounding privatisation and the other matters raised by Obasanjo. Then publish the documentary evidence supporting the claim that the Obasanjo administration recovered $2.8 billion under the panel Atiku says he chaired. If the accusations are false, documentation can help destroy them. If the historical record is more complicated, Nigerians deserve to know that too. This would be far more powerful than political speeches. AND WHAT SHOULD OBASANJO BE ASKED? Accountability must run in both directions. If Obasanjo wants Nigerians to accept his judgment of Atiku, Nigerians should also ask Obasanjo difficult questions. Why did he continue working with Atiku after allegedly discovering these problems? Why did his administration not secure a criminal conviction? Why did he later reconcile politically with Atiku? Why did he support Atiku in certain political circumstances after their bitter confrontation? And what documentary evidence supports the most serious allegations in My Watch? The Nigerian people should not be required to choose between two personalities. They should be given evidence. THE PRESIDENTIAL STANDARD The presidency should require more than the absence of a criminal conviction. It should require demonstrated integrity. It should require transparency. It should require sound judgment. It should require the ability to explain one’s financial and political history. It should require the humility to acknowledge mistakes. And it should require the courage to open controversial chapters of one’s public life to independent scrutiny. That standard applies to Atiku. But it must also apply to Tinubu. It must apply to Peter Obi. It must apply to every presidential candidate. THE FINAL QUESTION FOR ATIKU Atiku Abubakar does not need Nigerians to believe that Olusegun Obasanjo is perfect. He needs to persuade Nigerians that he himself is worthy of their trust. That is a different argument. Obasanjo may have political motives. He may have personal grievances. He may have changed his views over time. All of that is possible. But none of it answers the documentary questions surrounding the controversies of the Obasanjo years. The 2027 election should therefore put one question directly before Atiku: Why should Nigerians entrust the presidency to you when the president you served beside for eight years has repeatedly raised questions about your judgment, loyalty, transparency and integrity—and what documentary evidence can you provide that conclusively answers those questions? Atiku should answer that question. Not with insults. Not with nostalgia. Not with ethnicity. Not with religion. Not with political alliances. Not with campaign slogans. With evidence. And if he can provide compelling evidence, Nigerians should examine it. If he cannot, Nigerians should ask why. That is not persecution. That is democracy. NIGERIA DESERVES A PRESIDENT WHO CAN SURVIVE THE LIGHT The Nigerian presidency is too important to be decided by mythology. Tinubu’s record must be examined. Obi’s record must be examined. Atiku’s record must be examined. The test must be identical: Show us the record. Show us the money. Show us the policy. Show us the results. Show us the evidence. Then let Nigerians decide. The 2027 election should not be a referendum on who can tell the most convincing story about himself. [Africa’s Currency Question: What Would America Gain—or Lose—If Africa Learned to Trade With Itself? A new economic, security and geopolitical bargain between Africa and the United States By Jide Adesina | 1stAfrika.com The most important question in the debate over African monetary integration is not whether Africa should “destroy the dollar.” It is whether Africa can become economically integrated enough to rely less on foreign currencies for its internal commerce—while becoming prosperous enough to buy far more from the United States and the rest of the world. That distinction matters. Africa does not need to overthrow the dollar. The United States does not need to fear stronger African currencies. And Africa does not need to exchange one external patron for another. What Africa needs is economic sovereignty without isolation. What the United States needs is to recognize that a more self-reliant Africa could become not a weaker client, but a larger market, a more capable security partner, a deeper investment destination, and one of America’s most important commercial relationships of the twenty-first century. The currency debate is therefore not fundamentally about banknotes. It is about production, trade, debt, infrastructure, migration, security, resources, industrialization, political accountability, and Africa’s place in the global economy. The real question is simple: Can Africa build an economy strong enough to give its people, businesses and governments more choices? Nkrumah’s unfinished argument More than six decades ago, Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah, argued that political independence without economic integration would leave African countries vulnerable to outside control. In his 1963 address to the newly created Organization of African Unity, Nkrumah advocated greater continental coordination, including monetary cooperation, common economic institutions and eventually a unified African political and financial architecture. His point was not merely symbolic. A country may be politically independent and still remain economically dependent if its production, trade routes, strategic resources, financial system and development finance are controlled elsewhere. That remains true today. African economies often export commodities priced in foreign currencies, borrow in foreign currencies, import machinery and finished goods priced in foreign currencies, and settle significant trade through financial systems located outside the continent. The result is a persistent vulnerability: Africa earns hard currency from natural resources and agricultural exports, but often needs that same foreign currency to buy the technology, medicine, fuel, equipment and industrial inputs required for development. That is why the debate is not simply about replacing the dollar. It is about reducing excessive dependence on any currency or external financial system. Gaddafi, the gold dinar and historical caution No modern discussion of African monetary sovereignty can avoid Muammar Gaddafi. The former Libyan leader strongly supported African political and economic integration. He promoted the development of continental financial institutions and was associated with proposals for a more independent African monetary order. After his death in 2011, a powerful narrative emerged: that NATO intervened in Libya primarily to stop Gaddafi from launching a gold-backed African currency that would challenge the dollar and the CFA franc. The claim is politically compelling, but it should not be treated as settled history. There is evidence that Gaddafi favored greater African monetary independence and that some documents associated with the Libya conflict referred to possible plans for an African currency. But the available evidence does not establish that preventing a gold-backed currency was the decisive cause of NATO intervention or Gaddafi’s death. The more defensible conclusion is also the more important one: African monetary sovereignty would have geopolitical consequences because it would increase Africa’s bargaining power. A continent that can finance infrastructure through deeper local capital markets, process more of its own resources, settle more regional trade internally, and build credible regional reserve systems will negotiate differently with Washington, Beijing, Brussels, Moscow and the Gulf states. That is not anti-American. It is what sovereignty looks like in practice. The dollar is not Africa’s enemy The dollar remains dominant because it offers what global markets value: liquidity, convertibility, trusted legal and financial infrastructure, deep capital markets, widely accepted payment channels, and access to the world’s largest pool of investable assets. In the first quarter of 2026, the dollar accounted for 57.13% of global foreign-exchange reserves in the IMF’s COFER data.[imf] That dominance gives Washington considerable geopolitical and financial influence. It also gives African governments, companies and investors access to a highly liquid international currency. A company importing machinery from the United States can transact in dollars. An African sovereign can raise capital in global markets. An exporter can sell commodities through internationally recognized settlement systems. Banks can hold dollar assets as part of reserve and liquidity management. The problem is not the existence of the dollar. The problem is excessive dollar dependence in economies that earn largely in local currency but owe debts, import critical goods or finance infrastructure in foreign currency. When local currencies depreciate, the domestic cost of servicing dollar debt rises. Governments face fiscal stress. Banks and companies face balance-sheet pressure. Central banks lose room to maneuver. Households eventually absorb the consequences through inflation, reduced public services, or unemployment. Africa’s currency challenge is therefore less ideological than practical. It is about reducing currency mismatches and expanding economic choice. Africa’s real problem is production A common currency cannot rescue an economy that does not produce enough. If Africa created a single currency tomorrow without addressing energy shortages, infrastructure gaps, weak tax systems, uneven productivity, fragmented capital markets, governance failures, trade barriers and fiscal indiscipline, it could create a continental monetary crisis rather than continental prosperity. The lesson from Europe is instructive. The euro created a major monetary zone, but its members still differ sharply in productivity, fiscal capacity, debt levels and economic structure. Monetary integration without sufficiently strong fiscal and economic convergence can create persistent tensions. Africa is even more diverse. Nigeria’s economic structure differs from Rwanda’s. South Africa’s industrial base differs from Senegal’s. Egypt, Morocco, Kenya, Angola, Botswana and the Democratic Republic of Congo face radically different combinations of commodity exposure, demographics, fiscal capacity, infrastructure and financial development. A country facing an oil-price collapse does not necessarily need the same monetary policy as a country experiencing a manufacturing boom. That is why Africa should not begin with the slogan, “One currency now.” It should begin with a more serious objective: Build the economic architecture that could eventually sustain monetary union. Trade must come before the currency The African Continental Free Trade Area may be more important in the near term than a future African banknote. Africa’s internal trade remains low relative to other major regions. The African Development Bank reported that intra-African trade represented only about 14.4% of Africa’s total trade, reflecting fragmented production networks, weak cross-border infrastructure and persistent barriers to regional commerce.[afdb] That number reveals the deeper problem. Africa is not poor because it lacks resources. It is poor because it has not captured enough value from those resources through integrated production systems. The continent exports crude oil while importing refined fuels and petrochemicals. It exports cocoa while importing high-value chocolate and consumer products. It exports lithium, cobalt, copper and manganese but captures too little of the downstream value created in batteries, electric vehicles, electronics and advanced manufacturing. It exports cotton while importing finished garments. It exports agricultural commodities while importing processed food. The remedy is not monetary symbolism. It is industrial capability. Africa needs more regional value chains, reliable energy, ports, railways, roads, digital payment systems, manufacturing clusters, agricultural processing, pharmaceutical production, technical skills, research institutions and long-term industrial finance. A currency becomes credible because the economy behind it is credible. No central bank can permanently compensate for a continent that imports too much, produces too little and lacks the institutional capacity to manage its finances. Why America should welcome a stronger Africa A more integrated African monetary system would reduce some demand for the dollar in intra-African trade. It could diminish transaction revenues for some foreign banks and reduce a measure of Washington’s financial leverage. Those losses are real. But they are likely to be smaller than the gains from a richer and more productive African market. In 2025, U.S. goods trade with Sub-Saharan Africa totaled approximately $56.4 billion. U.S. services trade with the region totaled about $23.1 billion.[ustr] Those are significant figures, but they remain modest compared with the long-term opportunity represented by Africa’s demographics, urbanization, rising consumer markets, technology adoption and infrastructure needs. Africa’s population surpassed 1.5 billion in 2024 and is projected to approach 2.5 billion by 2050. The economic significance is not merely population growth. It is the expansion of a workforce, consumer base and entrepreneurial class that could reshape global demand.[uneca] A wealthier Africa would buy more software, medical technology, cloud services, agricultural technology, industrial equipment, aviation products, financial services, cybersecurity tools, educational services and entertainment. America’s strategic mistake would be to confuse African independence with anti-Americanism. A more prosperous Africa would not necessarily buy less from the United States. It could buy substantially more. What the United States could do The United States should not seek to obstruct African monetary integration. It should help make African economic integration more credible, transparent and commercially viable. An effective Africa policy would focus less on dependency and more on capacity. • Support interoperable African payment systems and secure digital financial infrastructure. • Expand local-currency financing for viable infrastructure and private-sector investment. • Help deepen African capital markets and strengthen financial-sector regulation. • Invest in industrial corridors, logistics networks and reliable electricity. • Build partnerships around African critical-mineral processing, rather than simply extraction. • Support technical training, scientific research and manufacturing capability. • Encourage U.S. firms to establish production, research and service operations across African markets. • Build investment frameworks that are transparent, rules-based and resistant to corruption. • Treat African governments as economic partners rather than aid recipients. This is not charity. It is strategic self-interest. A United States that helps African economies become more capable, more integrated and more productive will gain access to stronger markets, more resilient supply chains and more stable partners. The limits of a currency union Africa would gain from better regional settlement systems, local-currency trade, stronger cross-border payment infrastructure and deeper domestic capital markets. But a continental currency would also involve major risks. Countries would lose some ability to use exchange rates and national monetary policy to respond to local shocks. A financially reckless government could create pressure across the union. Inflation in a major economy could become a regional problem. Stronger economies could face political resistance if they are seen as permanently financing weaker ones. A credible African monetary union would therefore require far more than an African Central Bank. It would require: • Clear fiscal rules and credible enforcement. • Independent central-bank governance. • Transparent reserve management and audited accounts. • Strong banking supervision. • Reliable cross-border payment and settlement systems. • Deposit protection and crisis-resolution mechanisms. • Economic-convergence targets. • Rules limiting political financing by central banks. • Institutions capable of managing regional economic shocks. • Public confidence that monetary policy serves citizens rather than political elites. Without these safeguards, a continental currency could become a grand political symbol with weak economic foundations. Jobs, migration and security The strongest argument for African economic integration is not currency. It is employment. Sub-Saharan Africa’s working-age population is expected to expand by more than 600 million over the next quarter-century. Yet wage-paying work remains scarce: the World Bank reports that wage-paying employment accounts for only about 24% of employment in the region.[worldbank +1] This is the real migration equation. People do not leave their homes because they dislike their countries. They leave because they believe their chances of building a dignified life are better elsewhere. A young person who sees no path to stable work, business formation, education, safety or social mobility may choose dangerous migration because staying appears more dangerous economically. A currency alone will not change that. But regional trade, industrial employment, technology ecosystems, energy investment, agricultural processing and access to finance can. If a Nigerian can build a company in Lagos, if a Kenyan can work in an expanding technology economy, if a Ghanaian can participate in a regional food-processing industry, if Congolese minerals can support battery manufacturing in Africa, and if young Africans can find dignified work closer to home, the incentive for irregular migration can decline. Not disappear—but decline. The same principle applies to security. Poverty does not automatically produce terrorism. But unemployment, exclusion, weak institutions, corruption, state absence and economic frustration can create environments in which criminal networks and extremist groups recruit more easily. Military operations may disrupt armed groups. They cannot substitute for jobs, functioning schools, legitimate institutions and economic hope. You can destroy a terrorist camp. You cannot bomb unemployment. The new Atlantic bargain Africa’s future should not be defined by opposition to America. Nor should it be defined by continued dependence on America, China, Europe, Russia or the Gulf states. Africa needs strategic autonomy: the ability to trade, borrow, invest, manufacture and negotiate from a position of greater strength. That means currency plurality, not merely currency replacement. The dollar should remain available. So should the euro, the yuan and other international currencies. But African currencies should become more stable, more usable and more widely accepted in African trade. Regional settlement systems should expand. Local capital markets should deepen. An eventual continental monetary unit should be treated as a long-term destination, not an immediate political shortcut. The United States, meanwhile, should understand that its greatest strength has never been that others remain weak. America became powerful because it built institutions, markets, technology, infrastructure, innovation and productive capacity that the world wanted to use. Africa’s task is not to imitate America’s history. It is to build its own economic capacity. America’s task is not to prevent that rise. It is to compete fairly within it and participate profitably in it. The final question Would the United States lose something if Africa settled more of its own trade in African currencies? Yes. The dollar could lose a portion of its role in African commerce. U.S. financial institutions could lose some transaction revenue. Washington’s sanctions leverage could be less decisive in a more diversified payment environment. But America could gain something larger: a continent of more prosperous consumers, producers, investors and strategic partners. Africa, meanwhile, would gain more than a currency. It would gain choices. Choice about where to work. Choice about where to invest. Choice about where to build businesses. Choice about whether migration is an opportunity or a necessity. Choice about which partners to engage. Choice about whether its resources leave as raw materials or return as expensive finished goods. That is the real meaning of economic sovereignty. Africa should not begin with a continental currency. It should begin with trade. Then production. Then infrastructure. Then interoperable payments. Then deeper capital markets. Then regulatory convergence. Then fiscal discipline. Then credible institutions. Only after those foundations are durable should Africa seriously consider a common currency. The African Union’s long-term vision already includes continental financial institutions and eventual monetary integration. The challenge is not imagination. It is execution. Africa does not need to escape America. Africa needs to stop needing permission. And America does not need to fear African independence. ## Tuesday, December 18, 2018


### The Origins of UNO Hockey

[![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiZOVLtEixr21sZjagHgkhKjHzR7u82ur4r1Nd3b903gmizDzs4nV42wGfOG8vkjQ89UJ9gdHf-DH9glX-GK7sD4j8J4FQ2qejwdm0hlRAfii9JUwTqy4K4Blad6TswRpmkVMCGAPodRLjD/s640/playersticks.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiZOVLtEixr21sZjagHgkhKjHzR7u82ur4r1Nd3b903gmizDzs4nV42wGfOG8vkjQ89UJ9gdHf-DH9glX-GK7sD4j8J4FQ2qejwdm0hlRAfii9JUwTqy4K4Blad6TswRpmkVMCGAPodRLjD/s1600/playersticks.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
One of the things that has fascinated me about UNO Hockey over the course of the past 22 years has been the nascent beginnings for the sport at the university in the 1970s.

  

Before I go any further, I want to thank the talented team of archivists at the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s Criss Library for directing me to digitized yearbooks and providing rare photographs of UNO’s club hockey team during the 1970s.

  

I touched on this topic a bit in a 2015 blog titled [“The Arena Origin Story (Part 1).”](https://mavpuckblog.blogspot.com/2015/05/arena-origin-story-part1.html)

  

In that post, I talked about the Omaha Knights minor league team folding in the early 1970s. Fans of the sport were left to wonder if they’d get to watch high-level hockey in Omaha again.

  

UNO Athletics was under the direction of Don Leahy at the time.

  

The school had fielded a club team since 1972 (research from the _Omaha World-Herald_ archives also uncovered that Omaha University played club hockey during the 1940s).

  

According to UNO’s 1975 yearbook, a student named Tim Rock decided to organize a club team in January 1972.

  

[![Image 3](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDEBRUaX4d3-TU39OjmNY0ZNE-Rj_lhIaiWXmPUN6vigZIG7-27ubkY6SUuAXWfvXkDfE3Czpz5z8Q472L4X_AFd3ESFAgrNFimixLQi6UM2jjRK-wKWuBFl48BwFy3fhV5EIMjGIpgZy6/s640/lockers.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDEBRUaX4d3-TU39OjmNY0ZNE-Rj_lhIaiWXmPUN6vigZIG7-27ubkY6SUuAXWfvXkDfE3Czpz5z8Q472L4X_AFd3ESFAgrNFimixLQi6UM2jjRK-wKWuBFl48BwFy3fhV5EIMjGIpgZy6/s1600/lockers.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
The UNO Athletic Department took over some of the costs of fielding a team during that era — providing uniforms and ice time at Ak-Sar-Ben.

  

The department’s business manager at the time, Russ Baldwin, said college hockey was a “growing sport” and that professional teams were relying “more and more on college students for talent.”

  

This image of UNO playing Creighton appeared in the school’s 1975 yearbook:

  

[![Image 4](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgCXwbvQwror90UG9Fzdeib4XOuU1Mbj-hx7qzuDCmtGXlC6wj06vO7KAv14SVB9eOHOc8Ld2vmxHRSV42RRRzHbhCABAQK9oDFmqd3hnHS6WVrK8FnDSyBjUJZZ7UyEoCwdXv5gv2eX4IW/s640/unocreighton.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgCXwbvQwror90UG9Fzdeib4XOuU1Mbj-hx7qzuDCmtGXlC6wj06vO7KAv14SVB9eOHOc8Ld2vmxHRSV42RRRzHbhCABAQK9oDFmqd3hnHS6WVrK8FnDSyBjUJZZ7UyEoCwdXv5gv2eX4IW/s1600/unocreighton.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
During my research for this article, I began to realize what a terrific opportunity the university had to fill the void left by the departed Knights organization (which played to packed houses at Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum).

  

A familiar face to UNO Hockey fans took over the fledgling club operation in the 1975-76 season — Duluth, Minnesota native Mike Kemp (who was only 23 at the time).

  

[![Image 5](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjw-Z6ep-SaioOP91HLXcbboaUaNz8i4ARvTokCSCDhFIsgHFGw8rE9TjoKsllO-WASQaasFggyEA2PW6uXIfw3tAdi8DV3tFxaH0WREbuKc3ZJ332HSh-kEcA8QOMcrBAdHikXKv1LW5z2/s640/kempwhiteboard.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjw-Z6ep-SaioOP91HLXcbboaUaNz8i4ARvTokCSCDhFIsgHFGw8rE9TjoKsllO-WASQaasFggyEA2PW6uXIfw3tAdi8DV3tFxaH0WREbuKc3ZJ332HSh-kEcA8QOMcrBAdHikXKv1LW5z2/s1600/kempwhiteboard.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
(Kemp’s current title is “Associate Athletic Director — Events & Facilities” at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Prior to being elevated to an associate athletic director position, he coached the UNO Hockey program from 1996 thru 2009.)

  

[![Image 6](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjRiWzxbwFHIUqA1v__gTHzlV4pGzxlgb00LL4D2VkExY5NNBITqtIzZ-dX6vFLnzud32Nd7mFX4e4OF5sdesIxieRFrzI8TdW3eY6u4bmQ4t7NrBPmuGBwhrwv4w94IyFMK16f-V2Ym8Zj/s640/chalkboard.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjRiWzxbwFHIUqA1v__gTHzlV4pGzxlgb00LL4D2VkExY5NNBITqtIzZ-dX6vFLnzud32Nd7mFX4e4OF5sdesIxieRFrzI8TdW3eY6u4bmQ4t7NrBPmuGBwhrwv4w94IyFMK16f-V2Ym8Zj/s1600/chalkboard.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

_Omaha World-Herald_ reporter Jerry Fricke addressed the state of hockey in Omaha in a column published on April 21, 1976:

  

_“Coach Kemp, whose club team finished with an 11-14-2 record, has been recruiting and arranging a schedule with the idea that UNO will go varsity._ _‘If we don’t go varsity, I won’t be here,’ Kemp said. ‘Most of the games I’ve arranged are with varsity teams, and they won’t play us unless we have a varsity team.’”_

  

[![Image 7](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhzayHRv9UMbGd8-5OgQqDOEebp_ffORBNTZb-hdby_HGmbtVRWYw0oBxEEiZAiT2RvCmdDkgj2sl5I7CU5rUaI5_51_Fm4qMZn2A_FeVARiyHQ8NpaHbcUtvDuzYpmnnqF3n7RU2bgduOV/s640/UNOvsUNLwalkonice.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhzayHRv9UMbGd8-5OgQqDOEebp_ffORBNTZb-hdby_HGmbtVRWYw0oBxEEiZAiT2RvCmdDkgj2sl5I7CU5rUaI5_51_Fm4qMZn2A_FeVARiyHQ8NpaHbcUtvDuzYpmnnqF3n7RU2bgduOV/s1600/UNOvsUNLwalkonice.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
Further research in the _Omaha World-Herald_ shows that a non-profit group had been set up to help raise money for scholarships for the club players.

  

A recent profile of Mike Kemp — [written by Ryan Jaeckel for _The Gateway_ on Oct. 30, 2018](http://unothegateway.com/mike-kemp-a-maverick-by-definition/) — unearths a few more details about Kemp’s season with UNO’s club program in 1975-76.

  

According to the article, Kemp had earned a degree in public relations from Gustavus Adolphus College in 1975. He was working in the family business in Duluth when he received a call from his old hockey coach informing him that UNO was “looking for a club hockey coach.”

  

Kemp told _The Gateway_ that his experience coaching UNO's club team was “interesting.”

  

[![Image 8](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNUIQ7wlbVy8kPFdP5GMKsUeDeMdmVN87_crllk6jcAJYfDUp5rX9Ebc33-CYZYJwkNuq07o0jKzvNktRK5p7LZTYboyiYzVWtBFJrfhD0Cb4Bap3lEKnqykOcsQHIH6a1AGkv7WeyiUbn/s640/lockershot.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNUIQ7wlbVy8kPFdP5GMKsUeDeMdmVN87_crllk6jcAJYfDUp5rX9Ebc33-CYZYJwkNuq07o0jKzvNktRK5p7LZTYboyiYzVWtBFJrfhD0Cb4Bap3lEKnqykOcsQHIH6a1AGkv7WeyiUbn/s1600/lockershot.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
There were players from a variety of backgrounds, Jaeckel wrote. "A 38-year-old from North Dakota working at Kellogg’s. Another, from Michigan State, was in their mid-30s and worked as a salesman for a major corporation. There were Creighton Prep seniors. Even Kemp’s closest friend, who had just returned from Vietnam, joined in the fun.”

  

According to Jaeckel's article, the "friend who had just returned from the Vietnam War" would eventually be involved in starting UNO's Division 1 program in 1996.

  

[![Image 9](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh_lGCvMJeLhvJ1u3UGJAOQ-WAwDn1sypGT3Dyo_FW30gSo1rpdMYsNfJePYi9AsNT1YNK3kXFfcKkrF4Wgzl_OUGTFXJF9GqvaL-5WSDQNWfUus-XDrajTsaS_4p8vD1lD4DpYE6LybWs2/s640/bench.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh_lGCvMJeLhvJ1u3UGJAOQ-WAwDn1sypGT3Dyo_FW30gSo1rpdMYsNfJePYi9AsNT1YNK3kXFfcKkrF4Wgzl_OUGTFXJF9GqvaL-5WSDQNWfUus-XDrajTsaS_4p8vD1lD4DpYE6LybWs2/s1600/bench.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
Kemp referred to that club team, "lovingly," as “the largest collection of human debris ever assembled.”

  

As I alluded to earlier, there was talk that UNO would move up to the varsity level for hockey in the 1976-77 season. “Kemp began recruiting immediately,” writes Jaeckel, “going as far north as Canada.”

  

[![Image 10](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi4zMfRCFzbTi-ciS7gXRoO6uTUUb8blsst0ixM-Pm3cNzX0aeiJ7pKzF4pGufRw-w_8CkFJW6PPyfBY5LPH7Idt9tyLski6p_DM_MqyeBD-QJA8QOM-FaxcbZ5jLH32Al40Nf0JeFiVXFV/s640/UNOvUNOAk.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi4zMfRCFzbTi-ciS7gXRoO6uTUUb8blsst0ixM-Pm3cNzX0aeiJ7pKzF4pGufRw-w_8CkFJW6PPyfBY5LPH7Idt9tyLski6p_DM_MqyeBD-QJA8QOM-FaxcbZ5jLH32Al40Nf0JeFiVXFV/s1600/UNOvUNOAk.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
UNO ended its efforts early, citing financial constraints at the time.Kemp left the university shortly thereafter, and the school’s hockey prospects remained largely dormant for another two decades.

  

There were other iterations of UNO’s club team between the 1970s era club teams and the NCAA Division I program started in 1996.

  

For example, the 1981 flavor of club hockey at UNO was led by a player/coach named Tak Soto — who played on the Japanese Olympic hockey team (according to the March 4, 1981, issue of _The Gateway_):

  

[![Image 11](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIEd9CtQ3_ohDCsA8VlYTLNkiOEY7xenWPCQIaI7TN7DG8DFTs-fA3ltlMWQJlSLzXLi4AG8OpcOL1BHr9ZXbOetYrjqd7oK_DjJj_07xxnRcYGd03GSmRW2heRaskR3bx602p20UieJex/s320/sato.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIEd9CtQ3_ohDCsA8VlYTLNkiOEY7xenWPCQIaI7TN7DG8DFTs-fA3ltlMWQJlSLzXLi4AG8OpcOL1BHr9ZXbOetYrjqd7oK_DjJj_07xxnRcYGd03GSmRW2heRaskR3bx602p20UieJex/s1600/sato.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
When UNO Hockey finally took hold as a varsity sport in May 1996, Bridget and I (both newly-minted graduates of the university) put down our deposit on a pair of seats. I sent her over to Sapp Fieldhouse to wait in line the morning tickets first went on sale.

  

The reason I did is because I liked the idea that UNO was doing something interesting as it regarded athletics, and because I thought it would help UNO build its own identity in the lexicon of local sports.

  

But I’ve always wondered “what if?”

  

Had UNO started varsity-level hockey in the 1970s, would it have survived? Would it be a program with dozens of banners and hardware from decades of NCAA tournament appearances and championships?

  

We’ll never know, but it is fun to think about.

## Tuesday, December 18, 2018


### The Origins of UNO Hockey

[![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiZOVLtEixr21sZjagHgkhKjHzR7u82ur4r1Nd3b903gmizDzs4nV42wGfOG8vkjQ89UJ9gdHf-DH9glX-GK7sD4j8J4FQ2qejwdm0hlRAfii9JUwTqy4K4Blad6TswRpmkVMCGAPodRLjD/s640/playersticks.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiZOVLtEixr21sZjagHgkhKjHzR7u82ur4r1Nd3b903gmizDzs4nV42wGfOG8vkjQ89UJ9gdHf-DH9glX-GK7sD4j8J4FQ2qejwdm0hlRAfii9JUwTqy4K4Blad6TswRpmkVMCGAPodRLjD/s1600/playersticks.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
One of the things that has fascinated me about UNO Hockey over the course of the past 22 years has been the nascent beginnings for the sport at the university in the 1970s.

  

Before I go any further, I want to thank the talented team of archivists at the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s Criss Library for directing me to digitized yearbooks and providing rare photographs of UNO’s club hockey team during the 1970s.

  

I touched on this topic a bit in a 2015 blog titled [“The Arena Origin Story (Part 1).”](https://mavpuckblog.blogspot.com/2015/05/arena-origin-story-part1.html)

  

In that post, I talked about the Omaha Knights minor league team folding in the early 1970s. Fans of the sport were left to wonder if they’d get to watch high-level hockey in Omaha again.

  

UNO Athletics was under the direction of Don Leahy at the time.

  

The school had fielded a club team since 1972 (research from the _Omaha World-Herald_ archives also uncovered that Omaha University played club hockey during the 1940s).

  

According to UNO’s 1975 yearbook, a student named Tim Rock decided to organize a club team in January 1972.

  

[![Image 3](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDEBRUaX4d3-TU39OjmNY0ZNE-Rj_lhIaiWXmPUN6vigZIG7-27ubkY6SUuAXWfvXkDfE3Czpz5z8Q472L4X_AFd3ESFAgrNFimixLQi6UM2jjRK-wKWuBFl48BwFy3fhV5EIMjGIpgZy6/s640/lockers.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhDEBRUaX4d3-TU39OjmNY0ZNE-Rj_lhIaiWXmPUN6vigZIG7-27ubkY6SUuAXWfvXkDfE3Czpz5z8Q472L4X_AFd3ESFAgrNFimixLQi6UM2jjRK-wKWuBFl48BwFy3fhV5EIMjGIpgZy6/s1600/lockers.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
The UNO Athletic Department took over some of the costs of fielding a team during that era — providing uniforms and ice time at Ak-Sar-Ben.

  

The department’s business manager at the time, Russ Baldwin, said college hockey was a “growing sport” and that professional teams were relying “more and more on college students for talent.”

  

This image of UNO playing Creighton appeared in the school’s 1975 yearbook:

  

[![Image 4](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgCXwbvQwror90UG9Fzdeib4XOuU1Mbj-hx7qzuDCmtGXlC6wj06vO7KAv14SVB9eOHOc8Ld2vmxHRSV42RRRzHbhCABAQK9oDFmqd3hnHS6WVrK8FnDSyBjUJZZ7UyEoCwdXv5gv2eX4IW/s640/unocreighton.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgCXwbvQwror90UG9Fzdeib4XOuU1Mbj-hx7qzuDCmtGXlC6wj06vO7KAv14SVB9eOHOc8Ld2vmxHRSV42RRRzHbhCABAQK9oDFmqd3hnHS6WVrK8FnDSyBjUJZZ7UyEoCwdXv5gv2eX4IW/s1600/unocreighton.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
During my research for this article, I began to realize what a terrific opportunity the university had to fill the void left by the departed Knights organization (which played to packed houses at Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum).

  

A familiar face to UNO Hockey fans took over the fledgling club operation in the 1975-76 season — Duluth, Minnesota native Mike Kemp (who was only 23 at the time).

  

[![Image 5](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjw-Z6ep-SaioOP91HLXcbboaUaNz8i4ARvTokCSCDhFIsgHFGw8rE9TjoKsllO-WASQaasFggyEA2PW6uXIfw3tAdi8DV3tFxaH0WREbuKc3ZJ332HSh-kEcA8QOMcrBAdHikXKv1LW5z2/s640/kempwhiteboard.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjw-Z6ep-SaioOP91HLXcbboaUaNz8i4ARvTokCSCDhFIsgHFGw8rE9TjoKsllO-WASQaasFggyEA2PW6uXIfw3tAdi8DV3tFxaH0WREbuKc3ZJ332HSh-kEcA8QOMcrBAdHikXKv1LW5z2/s1600/kempwhiteboard.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
(Kemp’s current title is “Associate Athletic Director — Events & Facilities” at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Prior to being elevated to an associate athletic director position, he coached the UNO Hockey program from 1996 thru 2009.)

  

[![Image 6](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjRiWzxbwFHIUqA1v__gTHzlV4pGzxlgb00LL4D2VkExY5NNBITqtIzZ-dX6vFLnzud32Nd7mFX4e4OF5sdesIxieRFrzI8TdW3eY6u4bmQ4t7NrBPmuGBwhrwv4w94IyFMK16f-V2Ym8Zj/s640/chalkboard.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjRiWzxbwFHIUqA1v__gTHzlV4pGzxlgb00LL4D2VkExY5NNBITqtIzZ-dX6vFLnzud32Nd7mFX4e4OF5sdesIxieRFrzI8TdW3eY6u4bmQ4t7NrBPmuGBwhrwv4w94IyFMK16f-V2Ym8Zj/s1600/chalkboard.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

_Omaha World-Herald_ reporter Jerry Fricke addressed the state of hockey in Omaha in a column published on April 21, 1976:

  

_“Coach Kemp, whose club team finished with an 11-14-2 record, has been recruiting and arranging a schedule with the idea that UNO will go varsity._ _‘If we don’t go varsity, I won’t be here,’ Kemp said. ‘Most of the games I’ve arranged are with varsity teams, and they won’t play us unless we have a varsity team.’”_

  

[![Image 7](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhzayHRv9UMbGd8-5OgQqDOEebp_ffORBNTZb-hdby_HGmbtVRWYw0oBxEEiZAiT2RvCmdDkgj2sl5I7CU5rUaI5_51_Fm4qMZn2A_FeVARiyHQ8NpaHbcUtvDuzYpmnnqF3n7RU2bgduOV/s640/UNOvsUNLwalkonice.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhzayHRv9UMbGd8-5OgQqDOEebp_ffORBNTZb-hdby_HGmbtVRWYw0oBxEEiZAiT2RvCmdDkgj2sl5I7CU5rUaI5_51_Fm4qMZn2A_FeVARiyHQ8NpaHbcUtvDuzYpmnnqF3n7RU2bgduOV/s1600/UNOvsUNLwalkonice.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
Further research in the _Omaha World-Herald_ shows that a non-profit group had been set up to help raise money for scholarships for the club players.

  

A recent profile of Mike Kemp — [written by Ryan Jaeckel for _The Gateway_ on Oct. 30, 2018](http://unothegateway.com/mike-kemp-a-maverick-by-definition/) — unearths a few more details about Kemp’s season with UNO’s club program in 1975-76.

  

According to the article, Kemp had earned a degree in public relations from Gustavus Adolphus College in 1975. He was working in the family business in Duluth when he received a call from his old hockey coach informing him that UNO was “looking for a club hockey coach.”

  

Kemp told _The Gateway_ that his experience coaching UNO's club team was “interesting.”

  

[![Image 8](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNUIQ7wlbVy8kPFdP5GMKsUeDeMdmVN87_crllk6jcAJYfDUp5rX9Ebc33-CYZYJwkNuq07o0jKzvNktRK5p7LZTYboyiYzVWtBFJrfhD0Cb4Bap3lEKnqykOcsQHIH6a1AGkv7WeyiUbn/s640/lockershot.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhNUIQ7wlbVy8kPFdP5GMKsUeDeMdmVN87_crllk6jcAJYfDUp5rX9Ebc33-CYZYJwkNuq07o0jKzvNktRK5p7LZTYboyiYzVWtBFJrfhD0Cb4Bap3lEKnqykOcsQHIH6a1AGkv7WeyiUbn/s1600/lockershot.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
There were players from a variety of backgrounds, Jaeckel wrote. "A 38-year-old from North Dakota working at Kellogg’s. Another, from Michigan State, was in their mid-30s and worked as a salesman for a major corporation. There were Creighton Prep seniors. Even Kemp’s closest friend, who had just returned from Vietnam, joined in the fun.”

  

According to Jaeckel's article, the "friend who had just returned from the Vietnam War" would eventually be involved in starting UNO's Division 1 program in 1996.

  

[![Image 9](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh_lGCvMJeLhvJ1u3UGJAOQ-WAwDn1sypGT3Dyo_FW30gSo1rpdMYsNfJePYi9AsNT1YNK3kXFfcKkrF4Wgzl_OUGTFXJF9GqvaL-5WSDQNWfUus-XDrajTsaS_4p8vD1lD4DpYE6LybWs2/s640/bench.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh_lGCvMJeLhvJ1u3UGJAOQ-WAwDn1sypGT3Dyo_FW30gSo1rpdMYsNfJePYi9AsNT1YNK3kXFfcKkrF4Wgzl_OUGTFXJF9GqvaL-5WSDQNWfUus-XDrajTsaS_4p8vD1lD4DpYE6LybWs2/s1600/bench.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
Kemp referred to that club team, "lovingly," as “the largest collection of human debris ever assembled.”

  

As I alluded to earlier, there was talk that UNO would move up to the varsity level for hockey in the 1976-77 season. “Kemp began recruiting immediately,” writes Jaeckel, “going as far north as Canada.”

  

[![Image 10](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi4zMfRCFzbTi-ciS7gXRoO6uTUUb8blsst0ixM-Pm3cNzX0aeiJ7pKzF4pGufRw-w_8CkFJW6PPyfBY5LPH7Idt9tyLski6p_DM_MqyeBD-QJA8QOM-FaxcbZ5jLH32Al40Nf0JeFiVXFV/s640/UNOvUNOAk.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi4zMfRCFzbTi-ciS7gXRoO6uTUUb8blsst0ixM-Pm3cNzX0aeiJ7pKzF4pGufRw-w_8CkFJW6PPyfBY5LPH7Idt9tyLski6p_DM_MqyeBD-QJA8QOM-FaxcbZ5jLH32Al40Nf0JeFiVXFV/s1600/UNOvUNOAk.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
UNO ended its efforts early, citing financial constraints at the time.Kemp left the university shortly thereafter, and the school’s hockey prospects remained largely dormant for another two decades.

  

There were other iterations of UNO’s club team between the 1970s era club teams and the NCAA Division I program started in 1996.

  

For example, the 1981 flavor of club hockey at UNO was led by a player/coach named Tak Soto — who played on the Japanese Olympic hockey team (according to the March 4, 1981, issue of _The Gateway_):

  

[![Image 11](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIEd9CtQ3_ohDCsA8VlYTLNkiOEY7xenWPCQIaI7TN7DG8DFTs-fA3ltlMWQJlSLzXLi4AG8OpcOL1BHr9ZXbOetYrjqd7oK_DjJj_07xxnRcYGd03GSmRW2heRaskR3bx602p20UieJex/s320/sato.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIEd9CtQ3_ohDCsA8VlYTLNkiOEY7xenWPCQIaI7TN7DG8DFTs-fA3ltlMWQJlSLzXLi4AG8OpcOL1BHr9ZXbOetYrjqd7oK_DjJj_07xxnRcYGd03GSmRW2heRaskR3bx602p20UieJex/s1600/sato.jpg)
Photo credit: UNO Libraries' Archives and Special Collections

  
When UNO Hockey finally took hold as a varsity sport in May 1996, Bridget and I (both newly-minted graduates of the university) put down our deposit on a pair of seats. I sent her over to Sapp Fieldhouse to wait in line the morning tickets first went on sale.

  

The reason I did is because I liked the idea that UNO was doing something interesting as it regarded athletics, and because I thought it would help UNO build its own identity in the lexicon of local sports.

  

But I’ve always wondered “what if?”

  

Had UNO started varsity-level hockey in the 1970s, would it have survived? Would it be a program with dozens of banners and hardware from decades of NCAA tournament appearances and championships?

  

We’ll never know, but it is fun to think about.
